subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REASSESSMENT OF COMMUNITY EMPLOYMENT STRATEGY PROGRAM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the failure of the community employment strategy program to date to accomplish its objectives and the continuing need for measures to alleviate unemployment and in view of the high priority placed on the program by the former minister of manpower and immigration who said, on April 9, 1976 in Halifax, Nova Scotia, "anything goes for CES", I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather):
That the Minister of Manpower and Immigration reassess the community employment strategy program and expedite its imposition in view of the failure of this program to achieve its goals and to alleviate, in a meaningful way, the need for the creation of new jobs in distressed areas of the country.

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF INFLATION BY END OF YEAR-RESTRAINT ON SPENDING BY ALL LEVELS OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. With this morning's disappointing inflation figures showing a three-month CPI rise of 8.4 per cent, a rate considerably in excess of the second year target of the anti-inflation program and even above the first year target, would the minister indicate if he is still confident that we will achieve a 6 per cent inflation level based on the implicit price index and the C.P. index by the end of this year?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I previously indicated to the House, we were anticipating the event which occurred both this month and last month; that is to say, an increase in food prices in the country. If we can maintain additional restraint and achieve a further reduction on the non-food price side, then indeed the target can be attained.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DATE OF TERMINATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to make several comments on the hon. gentleman's brief speech. Yesterday 1 showed the minister a letter from the secretary of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. 1 showed him Saskatchewan Wheat Pool documents which proved that he was being misinformed. When I asked the minister a second question about whether he would inform the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool that he and parliament did not take lightly the fact that they were being misinformed, instead of answering my question either by saying "yes" or "no" he went on to say that the matter of land measurement-

Privilege-Hon. Alvin Hamilton
in other words, hectares-was a provincial and not a federal responsibility.
I maintain that this was either a deliberate or unwitting misleading of the House. 1 would like to quote from the third paragraph of a letter dated February 25 to the minister from the secretary of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, as follows:
Canadian policy, unanimously adopted by the government of Canada in a white paper, 1970, calls for a planned conversion to the international system of standards known as the metric system.
That statement was made in the letter by the secretary of that organization placing upon the federal parliament the responsibility for passing a law which provides that conversion to the metric system is the law of the land. Mr. Speaker, you know, as well as 1 do, that no government white paper means anything until it is passed in this House by a vote of the parliamentarians present. It is a legislative proposal. In fact, before the metric system can become effective across Canada, 90 statutes of this parliament will have to be amended, and as yet not one has been amended.
The secretary of an organization wrote a letter to the minister and sent copies to members of parliament saying that this is an unanimously adopted federal law. The secretary of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool went on in his letter to say:
At the annual meetings of the elected delegates who represent the shareholders of Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, held in 1974, 1975 and 1976, reports on metric conversion and displays to assist elected leaders to understand the metric conversion process in agriculture, and particularly in the grain industry, were presented.
The secretary states the following in another paragraph:
During all this period, no resolutions were received from the 800 active Wheat Pool local committees or from annual meetings held, or from other membership meetings held throughout the province to discuss issues dealing with the operations or farm policies of this organization.
That paragraph was meant to tell the minister that the farmers were not objecting to the metric system. Yesterday, I sent six Saskatchewan Wheat Pool documents to the minister pointing out that local rank and file members at the district level and subdistrict level had submitted resolutions opposing the metric system. When I asked the minister this morning if he would defend parliament by writing to this secretary and telling him that there was misleading information in his letter and asking for an explanation, his answer to me was that the system of measurement of land in the prairies and all across Canada is a matter of provincial jurisdiction, which begs the question and in effect the minister is supporting that misrepresentation in this House.
Parliament has not passed any laws dealing with the metric system, yet officials of the minister went out to the provincial governments, to these grain companies to private businesses and to consumers' associations and said that this was the law and that they should get ready to put the law into effect by February 1, 1977. I simply point out that federal officials are misinforming the public through grain companies and private companies. The minister has the gall to tell me in this House that the federal government has nothing to do with land measurement in the provinces. I wonder who persuaded the governments of the provinces that this is the law of the land, if
(Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain).]
it was not the minister's officials. What I am trying to say is that not only are the minister's officials misinforming and imposing upon my privileges as a member of parliament and on the privileges of every other hon. member. The minister is not informing us truthfully because the federal government got this whole thing going without passing a law to make it legal.
I would like to conclude my question of privilege by asking the minister to reconsider his answers and defend this parliament. I would like him to point out to the secretary of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool that as parliamentarians we expect to be told the whole truth, and nothing but the truth-and not to be faced with this type of answer.

One of the main reasons was that it permitted nearly all the questions to be dealt with by subordinate legislation or by regulation. I want to deal with the principle outlined in section 5 of the act which asserts that no person other than a Canadian citizen or resident has a right to come into or remain in Canada. This is linked with section 14 which provides that if the immigration officer is satisfied that it would not be contrary to the act or regulations to grant admission, he may grant admission after imposing terms. I would call the attention of the House to the permissive word "may" which, taken with section 5, may indeed be the means of depriving the would-be applicant of rights. In the previous act, section 27, which otherwise corresponded exactly with section 14, used the word "shall" and thereby said that an immigration officer, satisfied that all the rules had been complied with, "shall" grant admission. The new bill says that he "may" grant admission.
Couple that with the general statement that no person other than a Canadian citizen or resident has the right to enter Canada and I say it is clearly erroneous to assert that no immigrant has any rights, since he will have rights until this new legislation passes. It is true that Canada as a sovereign nation has the right to exclude or accept whatever immigrants

March 11, 1977
Immigration Act
it chooses; but parliament has legislated, and where it has legislated it has conferred statutory rights, rights which indeed may be withdrawn but which are nonetheless real. The Supreme Court of Canada has frequently referred to these statutory rights. Therefore, clause 5 as presently set out in the bill is not only bad in principle but is erroneous in law. Nor is this merely an academic matter. Immigration officials and perhaps the courts may treat immigrants as if they had no rights. I find it strange that Canada, a country built on immigration, a country most of whose inhabitants came here as immigrants under unlimited right of entry, should seek to remove all such rights.
The repeal of provisions with regard to domicile is a backward step. A person living in Canada for five years acquired Canadian domicile and was, generally speaking, not subject to deportation. That is to be changed. It is true that the Citizenship Act has shortened the period of required residence before an application can be made for citizenship, and once one is a Canadian citizen one's status with respect to deportation changes entirely. But I remind the House that there is no absolute right to citizenship and there may be good and sufficient reason why some long-time residents of Canada do not wish to obtain citizenship. The effect of removing the concept of domicile from the act will be this: long-time residents of Canada who have established their homes, businesses and residence in Canada will have no assured protection against deportation on a wide number of grounds set out in the bill.
In the bill there are extremely broad and dangerous provisions with regard to admissibility and inadmissibility. For example, one is deemed to be inadmissible if there are reasonable grounds to suspect that one is likely to engage in criminal activities. How can one tell this? It is true that there is a note to the act which says that this provision will apply to those who, although never convicted, may perhaps be associated with organized crime. But the bill itself does not mention organized crime in this connection; there is no mention of it. It merely talks about people who are likely to engage in criminal activities. That is a matter of opinion. In whose mind will the opinion be? I presume it will be in the mind of immigration officials. Would-be immigrants may be suspected of such activities.
I say that a provision which penalizes a person because that person may be guilty of something, whereas he may be guilty of absolutely nothing, does not fit into our concepts of justice or into the rules of justice as we know them. Indeed, such language suggests guilt by association. If we are going to exclude people from entry, we should at least make sure they have committed some crime or offence which renders them not suitable for admission to Canada.
Clause 19(l)(f) provides that a person cannot enter Canada if there are reasonable grounds to believe that it is likely such person will engage in or instigate the subversion by force of any government while in Canada. The language of the law used to talk about subverting any democratic government. Now it talks about subverting any government: any govern-

ment now falls within the ban. Subparagraph (g) on page 14 of the bill extends the prohibition to those classes of persons likely to engage in acts of violence which may endanger the lives or safety of persons or who are associated with an organization that is likely to engage in such acts of violence. It is possible that a person might be a member of an organization but not be aware of all its activities; they may not know that in some parts of the world it is involved in acts of violence and therefore would be entirely free from any taint of violence or violent action. If we are introducing the principle of guilt by association and banning such people, or not allowing them to enter Canada, I say that we are introducing a novel and dangerous doctrine.
I come now to clause 39 which provides that a certificate signed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) is in itself proof of the matter stated in the certificate. Thus, the minister and the Solicitor General are given the ability, without trial, to determine if a person is to be in one of the prohibited classes. It is true that there is power to report to a special advisory board, but it is notable that this language seems to be permissive rather than obligatory. This sounds to me very much like the state of siege mentality which in many countries has resulted in the imposition of repression. I suggest that provision deprives people of their basic rights. No one, myself included, would pretend that Canada is on the verge of reaching the state of repression in respect of security matters which has deprived many peoples throughout the world of their fundamental human rights. I say that we should not start down that path by conferring on the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General, however admirable we think they may be, such vast and ill-defined powers.
At this stage I should like to deal with some parts of the new legislation which I think deserve commendation and should be incorporated in the final version of the bill. I believe that the spelling out of objectives in clause 3 is a good idea. That clause refers to facilitating the reunion of Canadian citizens with close relatives from abroad. I think that ought to be one of our fundamental objectives. It is said in the bill that any person who seeks admission to Canada is subject to standards of admission which do not discriminate on grounds of race, ethnic origin, colour, religion or sex. It is true that much remains to be done to give greater meaning to those words. One could give illustrations; unfortunately I do not have time to do so at present. However, it is useful to have the policy of non-discrimination outlined in the bill.
It is also stated that one of the objectives of immigration is to fulfil Canada's obligations with respect to refugees and to uphold its humanitarian tradition with respect to the displaced and persecuted. With those excellent sentiments we heartily concur. Indeed, I want to be sure that the statute law which will give effect to those sentiments will enable people in that position to come to Canada. I wish some way could be found to link some of the new objectives with specific provisions to enable their enforcement. It is all very well to include excellent objectives in the bill, but unless those objectives are supported
March 11, 1977

with specific, clear legislation and machinery for enforcement they will not mean much.
Clause 109 of the new legislation is most important. It provides for consultation and agreement with the provinces on the settlement of immigrants in Canada. It seems to me that the final authority in matters of immigration, if we are to preserve the federal structure, should be the federal parliament. However, there is a very great need for far closer consultation with the provinces so that immigration policies may be in line with the planning and cultural needs of the provinces of Canada.
I believe an improvement to the act is that instead of having special inquiry officers decide on the making of deportation orders, a new class of adjudicator will be appointed. Therefore, we will not have in the future the strange spectacle of an immigration officer preparing and presenting the case against a would-be immigrant and then going around the table and deciding the case, sometimes against the immigrant. There is an old saying that no person should be a judge of his own case.
I hope every effort will be made to separate the function of the adjudicators from that of their immigration officials. They should be judicially removed from the departmental administration.
There have been improvements with regard to the definitions. The previous act contained antiquated and unworkable language with regard to health and mental illness as a ground for exclusion. This has been altered. Although, as I mentioned, we question leaving the judgment to a medical officer, this represents a very real, considerable and humane improvement in the law. Another improvement is that we have got rid of the term "commits a crime involving moral turpitude" as a ground for inadmissibility. No two persons I have ever met have agreed on what are crimes involving moral turpitude. One person's moral turpitude is another person's pleasant privilege.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
I am glad that that phrase, which I think we borrowed from the United States, is to be eliminated from the act. I am not at all happy about the provisions in the act as they relate to appeals. At this stage, a right of appeal to the Immigration Appeal Board should be granted in all cases for deportation where removal orders are made or people are refused admission. I am well aware, of course, that there was a time when we had a great backlog of cases, but the classes of those admitted have been restricted. Visitors cannot apply in Canada. There is no danger of a repetition of the bottlenecks and backlogs, and the right of appeal should be clear and simple instead of involving, as it does in the present act, a whole series of semi-intelligible phrases.
We welcome the reference to refugees. We think the provisions in the act leave much to be desired. We believe this process should be simplified and that there should be a refugee claims board to which cases of refugee status should be referred. I have not found the present methods of dealing with
Immigration Act
the matter by the immigration appeal board and the advisory board satisfactory in cases of refugees. Some members of the board seem to have very little concept of what is going on in other parts of the world. We suggest that the refugee appeal claims board should contain a senior representative of the Immigration Department, a senior representative of the Department of External Affairs and a representative of the ethnic groups and of the churches which have taken great interest not only in the admission of refugees but their cases after they have arrived here.
Let us state with absolute clarity that applicants with refugee status still have an open and full hearing. Refugees should be treated as ordinary immigrants and not be required to make their cases on economic grounds. If they are treated exactly the same as other applicants, they get no special recognition of their status as refugees. That means people fleeing from political persecution, and often very great danger, from the countries in which they live and the countries to which they belong. It may be reasonable to say there should be some plan to look after refugees in Canada, either by relatives or ethnic groups, but the normal points system and the fact they should have to establish themselves successfully in Canada should not be required.
Where there are a large number of refugees such as the Chileans and those in Argentina, Canada should be prepared to send special teams to deal quickly with those cases. This worked well in the case of the Hungarians, the Ugandans and other refugees to Canada and it is working well in other countries to get people from Chile. From the experience of some of us who travelled recently in the Argentine, it is badly needed now. I regret the fact that the minister preferred to accept the advice of certain officials-and I believe they were rather junior officials-handling the present flow of immigrants and ignored the pleas of his colleagues in three of the major parties who carefully studied the matter and reported their views to him.
In conclusion, the question of immigration is closely connected with economic problems in Canada. It is clear that if we are to maintain our present level of population-and this would indeed seem reasonable in a country of Canada's resources-we will have to provide for a regular flow of immigrants. We do not recommend an open door policy, nor do we recommend a closed door policy. We propose a moderate assessment with reasonable numbers to be admitted which would be true to Canada's past as a country built by immigrants.
We are well aware that where there are high levels of unemployment and serious economic stagnation, immigrants are often blamed and demands arise for their exclusion. The answer to that is not a rigid exclusion of immigrants but the building of an expanded economy in Canada. We are a nation in an interdependent world. Our reaction to the problems of immigration will be an important test of our acceptance of this fact.
I have made it clear that we are disappointed with this legislation, particularly because of its threat to the principles

March 11, 1977
Immigration Act
of civil liberties. Perhaps, even more so, because of the wholesale acceptance of regulations and subordinate legislation as the primary means of making the laws in this field, a means that I explained yesterday is totally unsatisfactory. We will do our best to get the act amended in committee in the way we think makes sense. We will have to consider, and are considering very carefully, whether it would be consistent for us to vote for a bill which conceals as much as it discloses.

speakeroldname: Mr. Art Lee (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a deep sense of appreciation of the progress that Canada has made in the creation of a just and humanitarian immigration policy that I rise today to take part in this debate. I come from immigrant stock. With the exception of only two members of this Elouse, we are all the sons and daughters of immigrant forefathers, although some of us are aware that our ancestors had a more difficult time than others in gaining entry to Canada. It is because of that awareness of history that I wish to applaud the government for rejecting the recommendation of both the green paper and the special joint committee that the nominated category be eliminated. By that rejection, the principle of family reunification is maintained in this bill.
I noted with interest the remarks of the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) who spoke on behalf of his party. I have read his comments and have come to the unavoidable conclusion that he and his party do not give much importance to the principle of family reunification. He is against grandparents of any age sponsored by a Canadian citizen being included in the family class and the retention of the nominated category. His rationale for rejection of the nominated category is that they congregate in the urban areas but independents do not. I am at a loss to understand this reasoning. Immigrants and Canadians go where the jobs are, and that is why this government is placing much more emphasis on its stated policies of decentralization and regional economic expansion. As a Canadian of Chinese descent who is conscious of the story of Chinese immigration to this country, I know how important the principle of family reunification has been to so many families.
Before I address the specifics of this Bill I would ask your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, in allowing me to rehearse for this House some of the facts of that story which may be of interest particularly to those hon. members who are not fully conversant with the history of the west. Following confederation, Canada's immigration policy was that of the open door. Chinese workers were recruited in large numbers to work on the railroad that was to bind this nation together. My greatgrandfather was one of those nation builders. But by 1885, while a promotional campaign was being carried out in Britain, and to a lesser extent in other European countries, to lure settlers to Canada with 'subsidized transportation and cheap land, the government brought down an act to restrict and regulate Chinese immigration. The act imposed a head tax of $50 on each Chinese immigrant. Not very many Chinese peasants could afford that. A further restriction was that no vessel was

allowed to carry more than one Chinese immigrant for each 50 tons of its tonnage.
In the early years of this century, the immigration boom was on and promotion of immigration to Canada among farmers in Britain, France, and the United States was a major concern of the government. When not enough response was seen to be coming from northwestern Europe, the campaign to woo farmers from their own countries to ours moved into southern and eastern Europe. In 1900, however, a Chinese farmer wanting to emigrate to Canada would have found that the head tax had been doubled to $100: and to be sure of its effectiveness the tax was raised in 1903 to $500, at which level it remained, for the next 20 years. Similar restrictions were contemplated for the Japanese, but were prevented by diplomatic considerations.
It is now only 70 years-the span of one lifetime-since the 1907 anti-Asiatic race riots in Vancouver. Although the head tax on Chinese immigrants had drastically curbed the number of Chinese emigrating to Canada further action was deemed necessary to discourage the influx of other Asians. So an order in council disallowed the admission of any Asian immigrants who did not come to Canada "by direct and continuous journey" from their country of origin. A further regulation required that no Asian immigrant could land on Canadian soil without $200 in his pocket. This provision did not apply to Chinese or Japanese immigrants. The former were deemed to be sufficiently deterred by the $500 head tax, and the latter were to be limited in their numbers entering Canada by their own government. One could sum up the policy of this period and the ensuing 40 years as a closed door to any nationalities which it was felt would not be easily assimilated into the dominant culture.
The restrictions eased slightly in 1923, when regulations on Asian immigrants were changed to allow entry of farmers, domestic servants and the wives and minor children of residents of Canada provided they carried $250 in landing money. It was also provisional on there being no contrary legislation. This meant that Japanese immigration was still regulated by an agreement between the Canadian and Japanese governments. Chinese immigration was controlled by the Chinese immigration act passed that same year. This act, which remained in force until 1946, limited Chinese immigration into Canada to the following categories: diplomats and their families and staff; children born in Canada of Chinese parents who had left the country to receive their education; merchants, defined as those with $2,500 invested in a business in which they had been engaged for three years and who intended to invest the same amount in a Canadian business; and students.
Those who gained entry under these regulations could not change their status. They could be deported if they engaged in manual labour. They could not land at any other port than Vancouver or Victoria. Any transportation company which carried an immigrant subsequently denied entry had to re-transport that person and pay for his maintenance costs at immigration stations. A vessel could bring to Canada only one Chinese immigrant for every 250 tons of its tonnage.
March 11, 1977

When these new regulations were in place, the $500 head tax was dropped as no longer necessary. One student of the history of Chinese immigration to Canada, Dr. Wallace Chung, has estimated that if the government were to repay the $26,500,000 taken under the head tax law, the debt-having accrued at a modest interest rate of 4 per cent per annum, compounded-would now be in the neighbourhood of S159,-000,000. As a Canadian of Chinese ancestry, I think I can say that the sons and daughters of those who paid the tax would today count it a fair price for the benefits of being members of our society.
The Chinese immigration act was repealed in 1947 and Chinese became eligible for sponsored immigration in the same way as other Asians. The continuous journey regulation in effect since 1908 was also dropped. But through the 1950s, despite an economic boom that resulted in relaxation of many, laws, discriminatory regulations against Asians continued to be enforced. In 1951, Canada signed agreements with India, Pakistan and Ceylon to admit only a limited number of their citizens over and above those eligible under the regulations governing Asiatics. In 1957, when the economic boom died, the rules governing occupational criteria were tightened. At the same time, however, there was a loosening of some regulations governing Asian immigrants to permit citizens of Canada to sponsor their spouses, minor children and elderly parents.
It was not until 1962 that unsponsored immigrants from all over the world became admissible under the same criteria, so that finally Asians, Africans, Latin Americans, and Caribbean peoples could gain admittance as unsponsored immigrants. The effect of this opening of the door was not felt for some years since preference went to professionals, skilled and technical workers. But all residents could now sponsor spouses, parents, grandparents, fiances and unmarried children. Asian and African nationalities thus gained several categories under which their loved ones could be sponsored that had always been denied them before.
In 1967, the principle of non-discrimination on the basis of race or nationality was explicitly affirmed in immigration regulations for all classes of immigrants. That principle is reaffirmed in this bill, and the government's commitment to that principle and to the principle of reuniting separated families is illustrated by the agreement between Canada and the People's Republic of China on family reunification which was obtained by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). For that, the Prime Minister will have the gratitude of many Canadians of Chinese ancestry.
Mr. Speaker, I prefaced my remarks on this bill with a brief history of Chinese and Asian immigration to Canada because I wanted to illustrate how far we have come in Canada in buttressing and developing the rights of all peoples in a nation founded on respect for the diversity of the cultures of mankind. A lot of the credit must go to those Chinese and other Asian immigrants who were pioneers in more than one sense of the word. I know that many of my ancestors met hardships in making their lives in Canada, often because of a misunderstanding of their way of life. By perseverance and patience,
Immigration Act
and by the strength they could draw from their culture, they won their right to full participation in Canadian society.
The three doctors of Chinese origin practicing in Vancouver in 1940 had become 76 practitioners by 1974. The one lawyer and one dentist had become 29 lawyers and 32 dentists. In 1940 there were no Chinese accountants or architects in the city; but by 1974 there were 18 accountants and nine architects of Chinese origin. Let no one imagine that this growth was an easy process. At the same time as they were growing up with the country, the country was growing up with them. The days of the "yellow peril" are not only gone; they are now unthinkable within the enlightened Canadian context. Canada can now address itself to the consideration of an over-all immigration policy without calling up the spectre of racism or national chauvinism. I think we have all come a long way, and we have come that way together.
I had the honour to serve as a member of the special joint committee which took the debate on the government's green paper out to the country at large. I am pleased that the government has seen fit to accept the majority of the committee's recommendations. I remember at the time that the committee was formed that some cynics-and some of them were fellow members on the committee-decried the travelling hearings as a public relations circus. Our recommendations would count for nothing, these cynics said, because the government had already made up its mind what would be in this bill we are now considering. We were nothing but window dressing, they said. The majority of our recommendations are now proposed as law. That's some window dressing! I see that as a reaffirmation of the worth of the parliamentary committee system and as proof of the government's commitment to its employment as a means of making the processes of government both accessible and responsive to the people. I therefore congratulate the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) and his predecessor, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), for the hard work and dedication they have demonstrated in responding to the committee's efforts with the formulation of this important piece of legislation.
As I said at the outset, almost all of us are of immigrant ancestry. We are all aware that this country owes its existence to the willingness of immigrants from all over the world to take a chance on Canada. It was the immigrants who opened the west, who pushed back the frontiers and who formed the agricultural basis for Canadian society after confederation. When the country developed into a modern industrial society, immigrant workers made the transition possible.
Today we have to consider the role of the immigrant in our new society. The first fact that we must acknowledge is that Canada is not facing a population problem. Nor are we facing an immigration problem, as some mini-demagogues might suggest. We are facing, instead, a problem of demographics as more and more of our people leave the rural areas for the large cities. This is perhaps one of the most important facts of modern Canadian life, and its future ramifications will be

March 11, 1977
Immigration Act
immense. By the end of this century-only 23 years now-nine out of ten Canadians will live in the cities. We do not have a population policy to deal with the stresses and strains that this mass exodus from the farms will have upon society. 1 hope that this legislation may lay the groundwork for developing such a policy.
The determination of Canada's immigration policy must eventually intermix with the establishment of a comprehensive population policy which will address the country's demographic needs. We are now experiencing zero population growth, so that the role of immigration in our society takes on a new importance. I believe the economic considerations are not paramount in determining our optimum population, since the economy is self-regulating-we are all producers and consumers. With co-operation from all levels of government, particularly the federal government, the economy could be managed so that we could use immigration to offset a static or even a declining population figure. There is little evidence that immigration causes or exacerbates inflation or unemployment, or adversely affects our balance of payments situation or creates regional disparities; and there is no reason to believe that zero population growth is necessary to maintain our accustomed standard of living.
We can, in fact, manage our economy in order to ensure that we do not lose our equilibrium. We must have an appropriate savings rate, relevant capital output ratio, a sufficient rate of capital accumulation, and adequate technological enhancement.
One major area with which the green paper did not deal, and which should be of fundamental concern to a consideration of population policy on the large scale, is the effect of the present zero population growth on my generation when it grows old and grey. The post-war baby boom-of which I and a great many more Canadians are the result-has not produced a baby boom of its own. The base of the population pyramid is therefore no longer widening. That means a downturn in eventual capital investment, and no expanding work force to support me and my contemporaries when we reach pensionable age. A recent estimate predicted that whereas today about one person is on pension for every five in the work force, by 2020 that ratio will have changed to one person on pension for every three in the work force.
Immigration can have a determining effect on that prediction since the majority of newcomers to Canada are highly skilled and young. This was pointed out as one of the shortcomings of the green paper by Dr. Andre Raynauld, former director of the Economic Council of Canada, when he appeared before the special joint committee. I agree with Dr. Raynauld that the government should certainly take this consideration into account when determining the levels of immigration.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before our noon adjournment I was discussing the importance of the relevance of immigration in today's context. There are significant non-economic factors to be considered, and the green paper places these issues squarely before us. Our immigration policy must be shaped by our over-all national aspirations, as well as by more narrow economic considerations. In the old days, immigration filled the west because this is where the land was for the taking. Today, immigrants go to the high-growth provinces-Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta-because that is where the jobs are. Some people say this undermines national unity and they want immigrants to be controlled in their movements within Canada.
The ramifications of that kind of control on freedom of movement fill me with a sense of foreboding. What we need, instead, is decentralization of our industry, which I believe would not only do a great deal to ease friction over immigration but would be of great value to the economic health of confederation and thus to all aspects of our national life.
There is the question of Canadian nationalism. Do we need a larger population to assert our independence from the influence of the United States? There may be some truth to this argument, but I believe that Canada is certainly large enough to pursue its national goals. Our economy has undergone a profound structural change, according to some authorities, so that we are no longer dependent on the American industrial economic core and all the markets, capital, technological and other factors which this implies. Certainly, we have recently demonstrated a sense of renewed national spirit in many cultural and social spheres even without a rapidly expanding population.
This bill would enhance the role of the provinces in national immigration policy and thus ensure that the needs of all parts of the country are properly met. Each year the minister will consult with the provinces over government forecasts of the number of immigrants to be admitted. I am disappointed, however, that the government will not submit its forecasts to the scrutiny of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration. I strongly urge the government to reconsider putting its forecasts under the committee's review. Too often
March 11, 1977

the special joint committee heard the voicing of mistrust of the Department of Manpower and Immigration because of allegations that officials abused their powers by setting internal levels of immigration based on race. That mistrust could be countered by the government's willingness to open itself to scrutiny by the standing committee so as to demonstrate to Canadians and prospective immigrants that our immigration policy is non-discriminatory, just and equitable.
Of equal concern to me is the overdependence upon regulation in this legislation. Decisions which are not subject to full public debate will always be subject to suspicion and mistrust. Immigration policy inherently demands openness, and that is why I strongly urge the government to lessen its dependence on legislation by regulation.
There is also some mistrust over the proposed setting of levels of immigration. To some, that means quotas. I can assure those people that that is not the intention of the government in controlling and managing immigration. In establishing annual or periodic forecasts, the commitment of the legislation to non-discrimination-to "first come, first served"-must be observed. Once established, a level of immigration-which is an order of magnitude or target figure- may be overshot or undershot. It will have no reference to specific countries or races. However, I urge the government to establish a more equal distribution of immigration posts abroad.
Some people seem to feel that by setting levels of immigration the government is lending credence to those who want to pin the blame on immigrants for all our social problems. I am sure that most hon. members of this House have heard the erroneous view that immigrants crowd our cities, cause housing shortages, steal jobs from Canadian citizens and abuse welfare provisions. There is no evidence for this kind of racist error. Immigrants are only a small part of the tremendous influx into the cities which is straining some aspects of our social fabric, a fabric which we know developed out of a Canadian society which no longer exists as the Canada of the 1970s. Of course immigrants are part of the problem, but we are all a part of the problem. As the special joint committee said:
-immigrants should not be blamed for problems they have done little to cause, although they may have compounded them. Canadians worried about the quality of life in the cities should look elsewhere than to sharply reduced immigration for a solution to the problems of city living.
With regard to the false idea that immigrants have a disproportionate impact on social services such as welfare and health care, the committee heard no evidence to back up this popular fallacy. In fact, the impression was that immigrant use of such services is less than the national average since they come from cultures where these functions are traditionally within the realm of family responsibility. In addition, many immigrants come from cultures which have taught them to be too proud and independent to accept aid which they see as charity. Nor is there any evidence to support the notion that immigrants do not participate as actively as long-time residents in the work force. I am at a loss to square this idea with
Immigration Act
the equally prevalent and equally false assertion that immigrants take jobs from Canadians.
Some submissions to the committee alleged that immigrants, especially non-whites, contribute disproportionately to the crime rate. This in fact turns out to be true, but not in the way intended. A report prepared for the Department of the Solicitor General in 1974 showed that the crime rate for immigrants was approximately one half that for native-born Canadians. The inference one is tempted to draw from that statistic is that more immigrants could mean less crime, but I leave that to the "pop" sociologists. Moreover, it seems to me that those who argue that by setting levels of immigration the government is lending credence to those who want to pin the blame on immigrants for all our social problems, are playing with numbers. How is it a level of 150,000 immigrants is discriminatory, but a level of 400,000 is not?
The bill provides for three admissible categories: the family class, refugees and other applicants. The family class corresponds to the current sponsored category, but it will be expanded to include parents and grandparents of any age sponsored by a Canadian citizen. Under previous legislation parents and grandparents had to be over 60 or, if under 60, incapable of employment. The refugee class is, for the first time in Canadian law, defined according to the UN convention and specific provision is made for the admission of refugees. The bill also provides authority to establish when necessary, for humanitarian reasons, special admissible classes for people who are not refugees within the convention definition. The third category, "other applicants", is made up of immigrants who are selected on the basis of a points system which takes into account factors such as occupation, education, etc. "Other applicants" shall be independent and nominated applicants.
One category of the 1952 act which is now outmoded is the "inadmissible" category. The definition of those whose entry is prohibited has therefore been revised. Provisions such as the absolute bar against epileptics are removed. Instead of retaining a long list of health conditions governing admission, the new provisions allow for individuals to be judged on their total health profile. We have added provisions to meet the threat posed by terrorists and those associated with organized crime. Changes in the inquiry system to provide adjudicators, coupled with the new concepts of exclusion orders and departure notices, will ensure fair hearings.
In conclusion, as a Canadian whose immigrant ancestors experienced hardship because of an immigration policy based on discrimination, I am pleased that the government has brought before this House a bill which enshrines the principle of non-discrimination as a basic objective of Canadian immigration policy. As a member of the special joint committee which conducted hearings from coast to coast on the issues raised in the government's green paper, I am gratified to see the majority of the committee's recommendations accepted by the government.
I urge the government to give greater consideration to the formulation of an over-all population policy for Canada, and specifically I ask the government to consider a greater involve-

March 11, 1977
Immigration Act
ment of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration in the setting of forecasts under this legislation.
I urge all hon. members of this House and all englightened Canadians to continue their efforts to dispel the erroneous notions which some Canadians still retain about those who have chosen Canada as the place in which to fulfil their dreams of a better life.
As I said at the beginning, we are all newcomers to this country, but if immigrants can produce a nation like Canada, and if immigrants can become a great people like the Canadian people, we have little to fear for the future.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to open my remarks by saying that it is difficult for me to believe that what we find in Bill C-24 is the best this government can come up with in the way of immigration policy. Our immigration policies have been under study for a number of years. The joint committee on immigration received scores of briefs on the subject, and it also received tens of thousands of words of testimony on immigration problems and policy from a wide range of interested parties. Many members provided excellent input on what we feel should be the direction of Canada's immigration policy. Therefore, I am disappointed and disheartened to find that we are no closer to a solution to our immigration problems than we were before those lengthy studies and hearings. In fact, if Bill C-24 passes and becomes our new immigration policy, we will be more confused about this issue than ever before. The bill before us does not lend itself to reasonable and rational debate. In fact, there are so many imponderables and unanswered questions that it defies debate. But we must try.
We were led to believe that Bill C-24 would indicate the direction that an immigration policy in Canada should follow. Instead, we are more in the dark than we have ever been. We were promised guidelines so that everyone would be able to understand it and follow it. Instead, we have a mish-mash, a patchwork quilt of confusing and conflicting policies.
The main problem with Bill C-24 is that it contains too many gaps, too many unanswered questions. Like most legislation tabled by this government, we are asked to approve the skeleton of a bill and allow ministers and bureaucrats to fill in the blanks later. For instance, just to name a few examples, we find that clause 115 begins with the words, "The governor in council may make regulations", followed by 24 subclauses for which regulations await the pleasure of the governor in council. Clause 116 begins with the words, "The minister may make regulations", followed by 12 subsections in which, in this case, we assume the minister will make the regulations at his pleasure. Clause 117 follows along the same lines, allowing the minister to establish the pertinent forms for purposes of administering this act.
Mr. Speaker, the regulations alluded to in those clauses are just the things that we should be debating. We in the official opposition have been protesting against these tactics for sever-

al years. We have been pointing out to this government that this is not the way parliament is supposed to operate. No government should expect this House to approve the principle of a legislative package and leave the government free to fill in the blanks later. It is not the principle of immigration policy that we are here to debate and approve; it is the specifics of immigration policy itself that we are expected to debate. The specifics are lacking, and I strongly resent being put into this position.
Mr. Speaker, we in the Official Opposition want to know, now, how the points system of assessing immigrants is going to work. We do not want this in general terms; we want to know exactly how it is going to work. It is obvious that we cannot approve or disapprove a policy when neither the government nor the opposition knows how the policy will work. We want to know exactly what powers will be delegated by the minister under the new policy, and we want to know exactly the level of public servants to whom the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) will be allowed to delegate that authority and power. This is a potentially dangerous situation and we do not want that degree of authority vested in public servants below the level of deputy minister.
In a federal system, immigration must be a federal matter. While repudiating the view that each province should have its own immigration policy, it is imperative that the provinces be consulted. Immigration to Canada affects all Canadians and no one province should have special status in respect to admitting immigrants. Once immigrants reach Canada they are free to travel and settle in any area, and thus the province or provinces which receive most immigrants should have more input into policy. At present, Ontario receives the greatest number of immigrants and the large urban centres such as Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver become the eventual points of settlement. Consultation with the large urban areas is also advisable as they have to contend with the problems that result.
Traditionally, the spread of population in Canada has been a natural development. As our frontier has crept westward, jumping over the Canadian shield, it has taken with it the traditions and social customs of our eastern settlements. Thus, the traditional way of life and respect for law and order tempered the Canadian frontier and produced a less volatile civilization than in the American west, for example. This traditional and systematic development has continued. Instilled in all Canadians is an admiration for our traditions and law centred society. Today, however, there is an increasing concern that we are losing, to some extent, the way of life that made our country great in the past.
Perhaps one of many reasons for this change in outlook has been the influence of some immigrants whose lifestyle is often foreign to that which has been traditionally Canadian. Mul-ticulturalism is all right in its place, but individuals who come to settle in our great country must become Canadians. The American experience has often been called a melting pot. We in this country, with our often garbled approach, might prop-
March 11, 1977

erly be termed a tossed salad. The contributions of various ethnic groups have enriched the Canadian heritage.
In the past, the Liberal government seems to have used immigration policy as a political tool. Canada is greater than the sum of its diverse parts, and in our efforts to formulate a coherent immigration policy we must bear this in mind. There is the myth that has to be exploded with regard to Canada's capacity for accepting an unlimited number of immigrants. Canada has an area of 3'/2 million square miles, and a population of 23 million people. The Northwest Territories alone is an area of 1.3 million square miles and has a population of less than 50,000 people. Some countries assume that we are able to accommodate a few million immigrants comfortably, but there is more to this than appears on the surface. There are aspects to this that are not covered in the guidebooks.
At least two-thirds of the land mass of Canada is taken up with ice and snow, mountains, tundra, rivers and lakes and other natural restrictions on human habitation. It is true that more people can be accommodated in the far north than are at present living there, but there are few people who could survive in the north, and fewer still who would want to try it. In Canada, as in other countries, immigrants tend to settle in the larger urban areas, most of them in the cities that at the same time offer the best climate.
In light of the present energy crisis, not only in Canada but around the world, we must be more aware now than ever before of the problems and expense of living in the colder parts of our country. The plain fact is that the energy crisis has changed our whole outlook as far as concerns moving large numbers of people into our Canadian northland. No longer is this possibility a simple solution for relieving the congestion of our cities. One-third of the people in Canada at present live in the three cities of Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. In every case those cities are experiencing serious growth problems, but the growth continues. We have problems with unemployment, pollution, crime and all the other problems that come from overcrowding of cities. In addition, we are experiencing the same after-effects of overcrowding which affect urban centres all over the world.
Cities are established generally where they can grow, and that means they should have access to water, jobs, transportation and good agricultural areas. If a city is close to sources of good it will be able to provide easily for its own needs; it will be able to generate jobs in the fields of food distribution, processing and marketing. Unfortunately, as the city grows the agricultural lands around it disappear. People have to go further afield to find their food, and therefore it gets more expensive. In the meantime, the demand for the same food from other areas places demands on available supplies, and we have found that this can result in undesirable situations. Assured of a ready market for their goods, suppliers will put up their prices. We have also found that some suppliers will hold back supplies, create artificial shortages and put their prices up still higher.
Immigration Act
Major airports account for more land lost to agricultural production and industrial use. Large airports take up thousands of acres of land, and expansion programs take up still more. I think we can see, Mr. Speaker, that the relatively small percentage of the livable land space in Canada dwindles almost by the minute. This is not really new to us: we have known for many years that available land in the part of Canada considered generally as livable is fast disappearing. These things I have mentioned must be considered when we are formulating immigration policy. Plain common sense tells us that we have an obligation to consider the welfare and happiness of the people already living here.
We must take a close look at our own resources and measure them against the needs of our people. At present we have about one million people in Canada looking for jobs. Many of them have given up any hope of finding meaningful employment. If we cannot do better than that for our own people, we are holding out false hopes to untrained and undertrained people in other countries by representing Canada as the land of golden opportunity. Mainly for that reason, Mr. Speaker, I believe we are doing both ourselves and prospective immigrants a disservice if we lower the standards we expect people who want to live permanently in Canada to meet. If opportunities do not exist in Canada for people who cannot make it in their own countries, we have the responsibility to be frank and honest not only with them but with ourselves.
I do not know of another country which has an open door policy today. I do not know of another country which allows the wholesale immigration of unskilled people. That policy belonged to the past century, when North America was sparsely populated, when we had room for people and needed new skills and pools of unskilled labour. These conditions no longer apply either to Canada or the United States.
We must consider the aspect of foreign aid and our obligation to assist developing nations to look after their own people. In past years, before we tightened our immigration policy with regard to applications for landed immigrant status from within the country, we were training people from developing nations to go back home and assist their own people. Instead of sending them home, we allowed many of them to stay here as landed immigrants. Even today we are accepting people as immigrants who have been trained in their own countries with foreign aid funds, and this works against both the letter and the spirit of our foreign aid program.
We have an obligation to avoid draining the trained and skilled people from developing nations. Part of our foreign aid program should be directed toward enhancing the attractiveness of one's own country, instead of holding up Canada as a more desirable country than one's own native land. We are not doing anyone any favour by continuing that kind of immigration policy. The plain fact is that we do not need those people, and their own countries do need them. In the past we followed a policy of attracting skilled people to immigrate. Because of this policy, many of those left behind in their countries were uneducated, unskilled, often living in abject poverty, whereas

March 11, 1977
Immigration Act
those who could and should have helped to improve the lot of their fellow countrymen left, looking for greener pastures.
Canada cannot attempt to solve all the world's population problems by accepting an unlimited number of immigrants. During March, April and May of 1975 the Canadian Association of Independent Businessmen polled their members for their views on immigration policy for Canada. Of those, 62 per cent who cast votes in the poll opposed a policy of high growth for Canada, while only 34 per cent opted for high growth. Those opposed cited congestion in metropolitan centres, housing shortages, lack of job opportunities and the further destruction of arable farm lands.
Surprisingly, there was a lot of support for the policy of telling new immigrants where they would be allowed to settle. Seventy per cent of those polled stated that there should be some degree of control over where immigrants could live, while 27 per cent expressed the view that there should not be any restrictions. The vast majority of those polled expressed the resounding view that Canadian citizenship is a privilege to be earned. It is a strange phenomenon that the federal government alone appears to take Canadian citizenship lightly.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am concerned about the way we are being compelled to debate immigration policy for Canada. Unless the government is willing to fill in a lot of gaps in this bill, and unless they are willing to accept amendments, we are going to end up with a real nightmare immigration policy. We are being asked to debate and approve a bill that indicates how the policy might work. We need a bill with specifics, a bill that indicates how it is going to work. No other approach can resolve this important matter.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like most pieces of legislation the bill now before us includes ramifications that gave rise to a number of comments. I submit that when discussing a bill of this kind bringing improvements in the area of immigrant "accommodation", we should never lose sight of a basic fact, which is that economic conditions in this country must dictate the possibility of accepting immigrants. We must first ensure that Canadians themselves are certain of a decent living in each and every of our provinces. I have heard it said that by increasing population through immigration, taxes could be levied on a greater number of citizens and tax revenues could rise. This in my view is a preposterous assumption.
It might be better to improve the standard of living for all Canadians and then we could think of increasing the population through immigration. I think this must be the determining factor for immigration purposes.
Earlier I heard someone speaking of unemployment rates. We now have an unemployment rate ranging in some areas between 25 per cent, 30 per cent and even 40 per cent. We must then study the procedure used to accept immigrants. There are two aspects to take into account: first, those who

would not be happy in Canada because they would not be able to earn a decent living; it could be prejudicial to some residents looking for nonexisting jobs, particularly in this critical period of the year. We can say that it has lasted too long already.
I recognize that since the beginning of our history French Canadians and later English Canadians have always been the two major cultures. But we should not forget that citizens from several countries have been settled in Canada for many years. It is quite difficult to say how many Indians were living in the territory forming today's Canada when Jacques Cartier was exploring the south coast. Today there are Indians in every trade and profession and they still have their traditional occupations like hunting, fishing and farming. Many are doctors, dentists, lawyers, teachers, nurses, clergymen, industrial workers or practicing any other profession.
History reports that the first Jews came to Canada around 1759 with the army of General Amherst commanding British troops in North America. We also know that Canada is home to a large number of citizens from all nationalities who, for the most part, made various contributions to the development of our country.
I understand that all those factors must be taken into account when we consider the possibility of amending an immigration policy generally, because many citizens of other countries who are in contact with relatives and friends here, of course, want to come and settle in Canada, and those are quite normal aspirations.
But, as I said earlier, the main point is that it is up to us as leaders and representatives of the Canadian people to orient the policy as a whole so as to make the economic situation for Canadians better, more livable. We may then view immigration in quite a different form from what it is now.
There are also people rightly referred to as refugees. In all countries of the world there are groups who suffer a great deal, and it would be most generous of Canada, with its vast territory, and if its economic situation were sound, I always add, to help those people.
I received late in 1976 a letter from a lay missionary who worked in Viet Nam and Cambodia for several years. I even rose in the House to allow well-intentioned families to adopt young Cambodians who were facing all sorts of hardships in their countries. I remember quite well the kind of representations that had to be made, the time it took before decisions were made. Yet every guarantee was given on both sides. 1 know three of them. I have here some photographs of young Cambodians who are living right now in the riding of Kamouraska and, to give an idea, I will read an excerpt from the letter I received from this lay missionary of my region who is completely devoted to the cause of disadvantaged people in other countries constantly threatened by all kinds of evils, mainly war. Let me read this paragraph which states:
Thousands of families were scattered in this way, and wandering children and teenagers managed to get to Thailand on their own, starving to death or ill, after walking sometimes several hundred kilometers and facing the worst dangers. All the evidence given by those refugees is consistent. Only 2 per cent of the Cambodian refugees managed to stay alive and reach Thailand, others were shot
March 11, 1977

like dogs by the red Khmer troops who still have a kind of shadow government in Phnom Penh. Those refugees have lost everything, their property, their land, often their family and their country. Those who fled wanted at least to stay alive.
Therefore, it is on behalf of these young people that we brought pressure to bear. A young man of 27 met with immigration officials. I was even contacted afterwards to learn whether he was satisfied with his interview because he had discussed all these problems. What is Canada doing in certain circumstances through its embassies? Let me tell you what is happening in our embassies in various countries. Only recently, we had another striking example with a young French-Canadi-an woman from Levis who is facing tremendous problems in India. The attempts of the Canadian government have not been successful so far. It would seem this situation is not taken too seriously by our high commissions abroad, and too often, the money sent by the Canadian government through its embassies is not always directed to the poor who might need it, but it benefits others who could manage by themselves, because they are better off than those who are suffering in concentration camps.
I continue this quotation:
We do not understand why this country does not react in the face of such crimes against humanity. And why has Canadian immigration such selective regulations? Why do we not admit to Canada a simple citizen as easily as we admit a political or military personality? People with influence and those with financial means are always the first to be accepted as it can be proved in several cases. The destitute and the orphans stand practically no chance of being accepted as refugees even though they may have a worthy Canadian sponsor.
This young man knows the situation very well as he has worked several years in various sectors of European countries, in Thailand, Cambodia and elsewhere, as I mentioned earlier. He added the following and 1 quote:
We know that our country cannot welcome all refugees from Thailand or elsewhere, but why not practice fairer and more humane policies? Why does the government fail to denounce such abuses before the United Nations? Those who say nothing are just as criminal as those who perpetrate the crime. Killing innocent people is an odious crime but our country says nothing to denounce it.
Perhaps you will find that I have drifted away from the subject being dealt with in Bill C-24 but nevertheless these facts are indeed related to our immigration problems since it raises the question of the adoption of totally deprived children. For example, we have the case of a man from Ottawa who has been after the manpower and immigration department for the last six months trying to adopt a young child from Cambodia. Although he can give all possible guarantees, being a well known doctor, everything is blocked at the immigration department.
To come back to the bill, I should like to deal with some of the most repressive aspects of the legislation. Several new aspects of the law have provisions ensuring better controls at all stages over the immigration procedure, so as to protect Canada against terrorism and organized crime.
I am wholeheartedly in favour of that. We must also bar entry into Canada to all sorts of people who could create many problems. That is to say we must fight unlawful or unauthorized immigration. Basically, the Canadian government wishes
Immigration Act
to take advantage of the passing of this new law to introduce all the measures necessary to make immigration one of the most important socio-economic programs. This infers the possibility of controlling as best as possible the political and economic instruments pertaining to immigration. To do so, the bill introduces a series of repressive measures but we shall only mention the most important or dangerous.
I will therefore deal with the extent of discretionary powers. All the repressive measures are made even more dangerous by the fact that they are enforced by the minister but not necessarily because the minister himself will have complete control since, in practice, a great number of his officials will wield powers with a very wide margin of discretion and authority. Almost everything pertaining to immigration depends on the decisions of the immigration officer. The margin of personal evaluation and, therefore, of possible error is enormous. And, far from correcting the situation, the new law tends in fact to make it worse. For example, the most sensitive clauses, dangerous because of their consequences, clauses pertaining to national security, clause 19(1) subclauses (e), (f), (g) can be enforced when there is only suspicion of intent. These discretionary powers, whether used under the act itself or under the various regulations derived from it, have indeed presented problems and were the subject of specific recommendations by the Joint Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, set forth in its second report to the House presented February 3, 1977, pages 979, 981 and 987.
Let us now deal with the extent of regulatory powers. A great many clauses come into real focus only when they are completed by the regulations provided for in clauses 115 and 116. However, the present aspect and direction of the bill leads us to fear that the regulations will only add to the restrictive and forbidding character of Bill C-24. This business of regulations always create problems. There are several acts that we often come across when trying to solve problems. We find that such a section means such and such a thing. However, there are regulations, and often, they are longer than the act itself. This has disastrous results, makes the legislation difficult to apply, and is most inconvenient, especially as the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments has just called the attention of parliament to the aims of regulatory powers in many a'reas, including immigration.
There are indeed many unpublished regulatory instruments, instructions or guidelines which affect the rights and freedoms of individuals without their being aware of their existences or their contents. Moreover, the joint committee itself, even though it was instructed by parliament to examine all regulatory instruments, has been refused access to the guide and guidelines of the department for the use of immigration officials. It should be noted in this regard that section 19(2)(d) maintains the present situation by forcing immigrants and visitors who try to enter Canada to meet the requirements included not only in the act and the regulations, but also in the orders or directions made or set out under the act or the

March 11, 1977
Immigration Act
regulations, even though these orders or directions are not made available to the public.
Finally, we must point out that the regulations can be amended or replaced as often as necessary without being submitted for discussion to parliament. Now that is something. Should anything happen which might create difficulties, a group of officials taking the responsibility in such a field will amend the regulations. Quite often the public is unaware of the fact but suddenly a clause of the regulation is amended-to prevent, delay or stop something in the relations between immigrants and the Canadian people. This occurs in other legislation as well. I know more about unemployment insurance with its regulations which are lengthier than the legislation itself.
The way things are now the Department of Manpower and Immigration will not even allow the joint standing committee to control and check all the related bills, a task entrusted by parliament. All this, needless to say, leaves a great measure of freedom to the department and the government.
I shall now deal with the admission requirements. Clause 19(1) contains the main reasons for inadmissibility of those arriving in Canada. The categories established in clause 19 are considered the most important and normally cannot be disregarded. They apply to all persons seeking entry into Canada, with the exception of course of Canadians. Let us point out however that the terms of clauses dealing with national security, particularly paragraphs (d), (e), (f) and (g) of clause 19 and clause 27(1 )(c), are quite vague and general. So much so that the government will not be able to enforce them on anybody without that person having very good means of defence, especially since the implementation of those provisions will be left to the discretion of a great many officials, immigration officers, senior immigration officers and adjudicators, and will be based most of the time on mere suspicion, the consideration of which will be left to the discretion of the official.
That leaves too much freedom to officials. They are apparently invested with the necessary authority to render decisions which may prove detrimental to whomever may be in trouble, decisions based very often, as I have indicated, on regulations which were amended when it was deemed necessary.
With this in mind, we can understand the concern of all those groups fighting for civil liberties and basic human rights.
I shall deal now with the conditions for removal. Clause 27(1) provides that various categories of people who have been granted admission to Canada may be the object of a report. What is provided for under clause 27 is followed by an inquiry, as indicated in subclauses (3) and (4), clause 29 and the following. Most times this leads to expulsion. I read subclauses (2) and (5) of clause 32. One of the main new features of this bill aims at making the condition of the permanent resident a lot more vulnerable than in the past, for a permanent resident could almost never be removed, once he had acquired landed immigrant status. The new bill creates six main general grounds for removal, including the most dangerous one mentioned in clause 19 and clause 27(1 )(a). As for the grounds for

inquiries and necessary removals of non Canadians, non residents, refugees, visitors, etc., their number is a lot greater. There are 12 types of more or less serious reasons provided for under clause 27(2)(h), according to the minister's own admission.
The comments on clause 27 on page 19-I am referring to the news release-are to the effect that this will not prevent either removal or local banishment.
The new legislation does away with the concept of domicile. In this respect, the minister himself cannot help but note that the new legislation affords a lot less protection than the current one-I refer to clause 127-which states that the people who have obtained Canadian domicile in Canada under the current legislation have a vested interest in the protection previously granted.
Clause 127 states however that this protection applies only in respect of an activity carried out before the coming into force of the new act. Therefore, Bill C-24 sanctions the loss of the vested interests of all permanent residents now residing here, since they are no longer protected against any action taken after the new legislation comes into effect. It seems that the suppression of the requirements regarding residence is a kind of incentive designed to encourage permanent residents to apply for citizenship as soon as possible, since citizenship would be their only protection against deportation. Now, since the coming into force, on February 15, 1977, of the new citizenship act, one may apply for citizenship after three years of residence in Canada instead of five. That is why the minister states that the domicile concept is now obsolete, as he said in committee as regards clause 127, on page 69. However, we forget to say ...
