subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for having quoted the Beauchesne's citation. Naturally, I have little opportunity to read Beauchesne's citations, and I have noticed there are many of them. Still 1 can readily speak in general. In any event, that is what I discussed at the start of my remarks, namely the difficulties stemming from the restrictions included in the Immigration Act, and that is what we are trying to amend here. I agree with the restrictions intended to prevent undesirables from entering into Canada or to deport those who after years in Canada have failed to adapt to our living conditions; and here I am not talking about economic conditions, which I mentioned earlier in my speech, but of normal life in our society. What I do want to point out is this: in all regulations on immigration, there must be clauses intended to prevent all sorts of things, to give the advantage to those who do offer sufficient guarantees. I mean the adoption
March 11, 1977

of children in a demoralizing situation, whatever their country of origin, when here in Canada we have Canadian guarantees which, while respecting the rules, can protect those young ones. In such cases the rules should be flexible enough to help those little ones, who are without parents, to have a chance of resuming a normal life in an environment where they would be protected from the problems they knew over there. In a way, that is a good Immigration Act.
Now, to come back to the underlying unemployment problem. I fail to understand why at certain times of the year we must send for a lot of workers from various countries for harvesting in western Canada, in Ontario or elsewhere. As I said before, I am convinced that the Department of Immigration or other labour agencies do not provide adequate information to Canadian workers, young or middle-aged, who would willingly go there. I intervened personally at the manpower and immigration centre to try to obtain accommodation for workers who wanted to do the harvesting in Ontario, but nothing was available. There was even a young man aged 17 who left Kamouraska with $227 he had earned working on a farm at the end of his studies. He got no protection, no direction, no help from the manpower and immigration centre. He found a job, but he had to work very hard and take many risks.
Citizens from Belgium or from the West Indies are hired for harvesting in Canada whereas we have thousands of unemployed here. I am in no way opposed to those Belgians or West Indians who come and work here; they are apparently hard workers. But why not try first to inform all Canadians. I am convinced that a very high percentage would be prepared to travel. They would even appreciate it. Many young people come to me to say that they would like to go and work in the English-speaking provinces to learn English if only they could find some accommodation. This is not a matter of being paid more than foreigners for the job. This is an immigration policy I would qualify as being considerate. First of all, we should organize normal living conditions here so that all Canadians can live decently in a country which is wealthy, tremendously wealthy, as some politicians say. We know that Canada is a very large country, a vast and wealthy country. We just have to organize economic conditions in such a way that everyone can live decently, then if we have immigrants pass legislation to welcome them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by saying that this is a debate which I personnally feel I have an obligation not only to myself but to my constituents to participate in, for the simple reason that, in my opinion, this is the most important legislation to come before this second session of the Thirtieth Parliament. As surely members on both sides of this Chamber must be aware, since October 12 last when the session commenced there have been a number of bills which were somewhat less than of all-important national concern. Let me quickly add that this is not one of those; this
Immigration Act
is a very important bill to all Canadians, if only because it will likely provide the policy guidelines for immigration for our nation for perhaps the next 25 years. At least that is the impression I get from the various responses that have been made so far.
If it is possible to launch an important debate in an ideal or near perfect atmosphere, then 1 suggest that this was the situation in this House last night. We had received well in advance ample background material from the Department of Manpower and Immigration, from the many private sources who were interested enough to provide it, and also from the very extensive work of the special joint committees. Opposition parties, especially my own, have been very active in a widespread study of the entire subject and, of course, specifically of this bill.
I want to commend the minister for making perhaps his best and most important speech in his relatively new capacity as Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen).

speechtext:
I particularly liked the comment made by the minister, not last night but last month, to the Osgoode Hall law school of York University. I want to quote him briefly. He said:
The anomaly between the important role that immigrants play in our society, and the archaic, obsolete nature of the present Immigration Act, has worried successive holders of my portfolio. This has been particularly true in the last decade or so.
The minister went on to say in that same speech that the bill-
-is designed to protect Canadian society against danger, and to protect it against illegality. But it does so with full regard for due process and for the rights of individuals in a way that the present act does not.
I can only add that I sincerely hope and trust that the minister can indeed fulfil this very commendable concept in his new legislation. As he pointed out last night, Canada is indeed a country of immigration. I want to relate this general but very true statement to my own constituency of Medicine Hat. Indeed I want to relate it to a much wider area which would include all of southeastern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan. All of the development of this area, which is very similar to me because, after all, it is home, is today the end result of immigration.
I am reminded of those early settlers from northwest Europe, many of whom built and lived in prairie sod houses, and from the United Kingdom, many of them professionals who somehow learned to survive and live with the land under rather extremely trying climatic and physical conditions. I think also of many of my neighbours who came from the United States, particularly the Dakotas. Then there were the Mormons who came from Utah and who brought with them their great skills in irrigation and land use. There is no question that they showed us the way to a very extensive irrigation system in Alberta, almost all of which is in my constituency across southern Alberta.

March 11, 1977
Immigration Act
I recall very specifically one particular immigrant, a tremendous man by the name of Peter Alkberg. This gentleman was driven out of his native Latvia after the 1917 revolution. As a youngster at home I remember his worn out photographs of his family farm which had been ravaged by war.
All of these immigrants in a sense were the product of adversity and necessity. They could turn their hand to anything, they could fix anything, and it was this background and their tenacity in our new country that enabled them to survive not only their tough beginning but the ten years of drought and depression of the thirties.
I spoke in the House not too long ago of the very real possibility of another drought right now in all of western Canada and the northwestern part of the United States. I suggested we would all benefit if we read again the history of that era and the considerable part played by those earlier immigrants. We might also remind ourselves of the words of Harry Truman, in my favourite quotation. I think it is appropriate. He said, "The only thing new is history we haven't read yet". Think about it. We should read and re-read the history of that drought. The climatic conditions that brought on that ten year dry period can be repeated. I hope not, but the possibility is there and the signs are there right now. So much for a little background history which I trust is both relevant and interesting.
I want to turn now to this debate and begin by commending my colleague, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), for a very thorough and complete analysis, not only of this bill but of the entire broad subject of immigration. It is quite obvious to me that this presentation was indeed a labour of love for my colleague, and all of us in the House are richer for his interest and his speech here last night.
There was one short sentence in my colleague's presentation which I consider to be the key to my personal approach to this issue, and I want to read it. It is as follows:
Today we are faced with the fact that despite tremendous gains in agricultural production, the world's population is again growing faster than the increase in food production.
That is a very succinct statement, and I think it is the key to what our forward planning should be, not only in immigration but in the broad agricultural sense. I suggest that this very basic situation must be uppermost in the mind of everyone who is concerned with the population growth, and with who will feed the people, and where. After all, as my colleague pointed out, world population is now increasing at the rate of some 200,000 people a day.
It seems to me that in spite of ample publicity and advance warning of this debate, and particularly in spite of the green paper and the work of the joint committee as it travelled across Canada, very little public input is available at this time. In my constituency, I had to search for it. My constituency office conducted a survey in the representative areas in the city of Medicine Hat, which numbers about 33,000 people, and in the various parts of our rather large rural area. Once contacted,

my constituents responded readily, and I must say forthrightly. Most of the comments were very specific and almost brutally frank. By some people's standards they might even be considered bigoted. I should like to quote some of these remarks that I obtained in the survey. The comment of a city housewife was:
Immigrants should not be allowed in, if once they get here, they have to go on welfare.
She followed up by saying that:
All immigrants should be screened to make sure they believe and support the democratic process.
A city businessman had this to say:
I do not favour a wide open policy. If we have a labour problem today, it is with menial labour, dishwashers, ditch diggers, etc. Therefore we cannot restrict immigration to skilled labour.
Another comment was:
If we allow immigrants into the country, we must be able to supply them with jobs.
A professional man said, rather bluntly:
No coloured people at all.
A lawyer had this to say:
Our policy must be far stricter, with stronger screening, and no draft evaders or political activists from South America or political refugees in general.
That was the bluntest of the statements that I received.
A highly proficient farmer feels there is a danger in making our policy too restrictive because we would deny ourselves a source of new ideas. He feels that new immigrants have a greater appreciation of our country than those native born. He feels our policy should allow for a small percentage of unskilled labour.
There was the repeated comment that existing regulations are too generous in that many more than close relatives, often complete small villages, have somehow managed to arrive here. Others pointed out that we should look at the problems in the United Kingdom's immigration policy and the situation there at present. A provincial civil servant pointed out the difficulty of a broadly based immigration policy without being quite selective. He feels there should be a carefully controlled policy with emphasis on skills. There was some critical comment from several farmers concerning new immigrants with access to much cheaper capital financing from foreign countries, and examples of this were given. Of course this would be a major advantage in acquiring farm land.
I want to emphasize that this constituency survey did not pose specific questions but asked for any comments that might be offered. No leading questions were put. With the single exception already noted, the general response called for stricter controls with more attention given to current abuses. I must say that I agree in general with the response.
Another unanimous response, especially from the farming sector of my constituency, was that Canada should help starving peoples in their own countries by providing suitable, practical help designed to promote an agricultural self-help policy. Again I fully support this approach.
March 11, 1977

I should like to speak now about a related manpower issue within the intensive irrigation districts of southern Alberta, and particularly the area which produces sugar beets. There was solid support for the existing provision to bring in temporary workers. In this case they were referring to the Mexican workers who are available in the summer for thinning the sugar beet crop in its early growth stage. This source of temporary help has replaced our own native people who at one time provided most of this type of labour. There is a clear indication that this foreign source of labour is more dependable and more productive. This is a serious statement to make, but it is the truth. It should be pointed out here that this kind of farm labour is superior to our Canadian born labour force which just will not do this kind of work. This temporary work policy should be continued.
There has already been ample comment on the matter of the regulations to be put forward with this new bill. I share the sentiments of my colleague, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), that we should have the regulations before us now for a proper second reading debate. After all it will be the regulations that will determine the degree of an open door or repressive policy for the immigration guidelines until the year 2000. It is the policy which is now under debate.
There is an interesting comparison here that 1 cannot fail to point out respecting regulations under another bill. This time I am referring to the bill amending Canada's Animal Contagious Diseases Act. That act was amended for the first time in over 100 years about two or more years ago in this House, and those of us in the Standing Committee on Agriculture had a lot to do with that. However, the regulations which spelled out much of the policy were not released until last January, some two years after the act was amended. Surely this is legislation by regulation at its worst, with the bureaucracy doing the regulating. I know the minister did indicate with a nod of his head last night that these regulations would be available shortly. Since that indication is obviously not part of Hansard, I must mention it again, but let us not try to beat that two-year record.
I also ask the minister that there be more positive provisions for provincial and even municipal input to take care ofTegion-al problems relating to the total demographic challenge. The provinces must surely have the final say in the matter of foreign students attending provincial universities and colleges, such as those in Alberta. Foreign students do enrich our universities, but the time has come, certainly in Alberta, when foreign enrollments in certain faculties such as engineering, medicine, and science, must be curtailed to allow reasonable access to our Canadian students.
I want to conclude these remarks with just a few further comments in summary. In an issue like this which is so important to our nation it is regrettable that we cannot all be members of the immigration committee or that we could not all have served on that special joint committee. However, it seems to me that the work of that special committee deserves
Immigration Act
our praise, and merits much use in the development of our Canadian immigration policy. I am sure my party endorses most of the recommendations of that committee.
It is obvious that at this stage in Canada's history we cannot allow unlimited immigration, and this means our policy must be of a selective type. The minister indicated last night that the right figure for our total annual level will emerge with experience and that this experience could very well be tempered somewhat with available housing. I hope due consideration will also be given to provincial situations and that a balance, if possible, will be determined between immigrants headed for Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver, and other regions across Canada.
It is worth repeating that immigration is a privilege and not a right, and Canada is much the richer for its immigrants. Is it not possible that our new immigrants, arriving as a result of a new and enlightened policy, might help to show Canadians the way back to a new work ethic and a new level of national productivity, which we need so much today, just as that first wave of immigrants responded during the first third of this century?
I and, I think, most of my constituents can support a renewed emphasis on immigration policy which recognizes standards which are not discriminatory as to race, nationality, colour, religion or sex. The method of selection must ensure that the right mix is obtained to be absorbed properly by our Canadian society.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on introducing the government's immigration bill the minister said that the bill explicitly affirms for the first time the fundamental objectives of Canadian immigration law: family reunification, non-discrimination, concern for refugees, and the promotion of Canadian economic, social, demographic and cultural goals.
I totally agree with the sentiments expressed by the minister in his opening remarks and I support them 100 per cent.
I would like also to congratulate the committee, as did the previous speaker, on the very excellent job it did travelling across the country, in listening to briefs from people from all walks of life and for putting forward a report of the highest calibre, which obviously met with the minister's approval since most of the major recommendations were accepted by him. I had the opportunity to travel with that committee only on the west coast, but I can assure the House and those hon. members who were not in attendance that the committee and its chairmen did an excellent job. It listened with a great deal of attention to the people who appeared before it and, as I said, it prepared a very excellent report which will probably shape the course of our immigration policy for many years to come. I congratulate the minister for accepting its recommendations, for putting them into legislative form, and for introducing them at an early date, which indicates to the House that he feels this legislation is important.
I would like to comment briefly on one or two parts of the legislation. One is that part of the legislation regarding the

March 11, 1977
Immigration Act
immigration levels which will be set after advice from the provinces as to where immigrants should go, as to what levels we can absorb at any given time, and as to what projects of a capital nature might be going on in Canada which might require specialized skills. In other words, this is a fluid type of policy. It is not engraved in stone; it is one which can be changed on a year by year basis if necessary, to reflect what is occurring in the Canadian economy. If there is one thing of which we are all aware, it is that we have a rapidly moving society in which factors change almost on a daily basis, let alone on a yearly basis. I think it is important that an immigration policy reflect that fluidity in our society so that it can cope with changing circumstances on a regular basis.
The second point is one upon which we all agree, and that is the importance of facilitating family reunions. It has been the policy of the Department of External Affairs to assist in the reunification of families with relatives from places like eastern Europe or perhaps Communist China. I must congratulate the Department of External Affairs, as well as the immigration people who have assisted me personally, in reuniting families which have been split because of political differences. These barriers are not made by God; they are man-made political barriers, and I think Canada has had a very good record for not carrying a big stick, yelling and screaming on issues of reunification. Over a period of time, through diplomacy, Canada has achieved not all the goals we desired, but certainly those which were possible at given times and under given sets of circumstances.
I solidly support the position of facilitating family reunion, and I suppose what focuses my attention on this bill is the fact that for the first time we have legislated the principle that immigration should be based upon non-discrimination.
When I lived in Yorkton, Saskatchewan, I recall that many of the people who ran cafes were, the Chinese who had come to this country when the Canadian Pacific Railway was being built. They were not allowed to bring their wives and sweethearts with them, and I recall that six or seven men used to live together in a boarding house. I thought it was a sad indictment of our society that they could not bring their womenfolk over because at that time our laws forbade such people of oriental origin coming here. It is with some pride that I see we have progresed beyond this. I am sure many hon. members would agree that, although we are not proud of that part of our history, we can be proud that we now have non-discrimination written into the legislation so that people may not be barred on grounds of race, religion, or sex. For my part, I wish it had come sooner.
We have had many discussions in this House about unemployment and the effect on the social fabric of our lines when people do not have work. I have travelled in Germany, Switzerland, and other European countries that have a lower unemployment rate than we do and have noticed that they bring people from Spain and less developed countries to join their work force. But during times of recession or when there is a
[Mr. Anderson.)
slowdown in the economy, these people are sent home because they were never allowed to become citizens. While the government may be accused of having contributed in some measure, to a recession, I take pride in the fact that people who wish to live in our country are not sent home in times of recession. I think we have reason to be proud of our humane attitude.
The Swiss set a limit on immigration and it may take an applicant ten or 15 years to come within that limit, so that is a less desirable situation. I know there is a group of people in Canada who have very strong feelings about immigration and feel that we should close the gate and only take care of those people already here.
I would state unequivocally, Mr. Speaker, that this House has an obligation to fight against discrimination by including a non-discrimination clause in the legislation such as that which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) introduced in his bill.
I was born and raised in Saskatchewan and I recall that in the early forties it was the accepted custom to bait people of Ukranian birth who painted Easter eggs and who spoke a different language on occasion. Many of them were born in the Ukraine and came to this country in the 1920's and the 1930's. Sometimes it was their mode of dress that gave rise to mirth. I would not say the treatment of them was harsh, but we felt there was something to laugh at. We could laugh at their customs, their clothing, their language but, Mr. Speaker, they were white.
I must admit that even today in my province of British Columbia there is subtle and not so subtle discrimination. I think it would be fair to say that the Chinese communities in British Columbia have experienced this, and the East Indian people. Perhaps they have run into the same sort of thing in other provinces as well as British Columbia as existed on the prairies in the 1930's and 1940's with that one difference-the difference in colour.
I think it would also be fair to say that up to November 15 in the province of British Columbia there was subtle and not too subtle discrimination against people of French Canadian origin, and certainly against the province of Quebec.
I see it as part of our job to do all we can whether by legislation, speaking in the House or throughout the country, to let the people of Canada know that we are totally opposed to any form of discrimination against any member of our society. I trust that with social and political maturity these forms of discrimination will become less and less evident as time goes on. I believe it is up to every member of this House to combat a very insidious decay in the country by letting our fellow citizens know that this House does not in any way condone intolerance and will not abide discrimination. Where we have the chance, such as in the legislation before us, we must point out strongly and clearly to the people of Canada that in our immigration policy we are opposed to discrimination, as well as in our day to day lives.
I trust that in British Columbia those very hard-working, law-abiding people who may be of a different colour from the majority of residents, will be recognized as the Canadians they
March 11, 1977

are. The fact that they work hard, that they believe in family unity and the importance of good housing, should not be used against them as though these things were wrong. Sometimes from the comments I hear I think these qualities are viewed as flaws rather than virtues. It would be better if more people followed their example rather than complaining that their industry takes jobs away from other members of the community.
It has been well documented that a reasonable inflow of people has not detracted from the quality of our economic, social or cultural life. The reverse is true. Immigrants have made contributions in the form of music, literature, and other cultural activities, so it is fair to say that these people, be they Hungarians, Ukrainians, Chinese, East Indians or what have you, have enriched our lives. It is a poor society that cannot look beyond its borders to other cultures. We have not reached the apex of our cultural development. We cannot afford to look down our noses at cultures which have been in existence for thousands of years and which antedate by many, many years, Canada's existence.
As I said, the non-discriminatory aspect of the bill is the most important part of the legislation. It is parliament's affirmation that discrimination has no place in this country and that we, as parliamentarians, recognize this.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think any legislation which will come before parliament in the present session will be as important as this bill. Whatever else we may say about our immigration policy we must, as a fundamental principle, refrain from being racist or discriminatory.
In the short time I shall talk on this bill I intend to emphasize that racism and discrimination really ought not to be the issue before Canadians. In other words, one begins by assuming that we are not going to be racist or bigoted with respect to sex, religion, colour or anything else.
Surely in the presentation of this matter to the Canadian people it is important to question some myths about the numbers of people we can bring into Canada. Therefore I intend to put forward two propositions, both of which are based on the assumption that Canada should have a restrictive immigration policy, that is, should restrict the numbers of people allowed to enter Canada. My first proposition is this: there is a myth in this country that we have all kinds of potential for absorbing new people. My second proposition, which I intend to demonstrate with researched data, is that we can best help the Third World by operating from a position of strength. With those two propositions firmly in mind, I wish to set forth my case.
One must underscore how desperate is the world's food shortage. The United Nations Advisory Committee on the Application of Science and Technology has this to say on the subject:
Immigration Act
Today there are over 300 million children who, for lack of sufficient protein and calories, suffer grossly retarded physical growth and development, and for many of these mental development, learning and behaviour may be impaired as well. Protein-calorie deficiencies also directly affect the health and economic productivity of adult populations. Such nutritional deficits, damaging both present and future generations, are built-in handicaps which must be corrected.
Obviously the situation is serious world-wide. We know that four fifths of the world's population suffers from malnutrition and more than 300 million children now suffer from permanent brain damage owing to lack of protein. In addition, the world's population is increasing at the rate of 77 million mouths per year.
In the face of these facts we should not react with a sort of knee-jerk reaction and say that, because the world is starving, Canada must have an open immigration policy. As I say, world population grows by 77 million mouths a year. If we were to accept in Canada every one of those 77 million people born in one year, we should make this into a country no longer able to export its research and technology. Furthermore, after one year the world would be no better off, Canada would be in the same position as the southern hemisphere, and the rest of the world would go on as usual.
The fundamental question must be, how can we best proceed so that by the year 2010 we can feed the human family of eight billion souls?
There are only two sources of food, soil and water. Canada is a big country, of 3.8 million square miles. It is the second largest nation in the world. In our land space we have some 5 billion, 312 million acres. Since we possess all this land, some Canadian people think that, somehow, we have the potential to feed vastly greater numbers of people than are already living here. In truth, only 24 million of those more than five billion acres are arable land in climatically favoured areas. Of those 24 million acres, only two million are class one soil, and only ten million class two soil. Even more significant is the fact that those 24 million acres will be reduced to nine million by the year 2000 if the rate of destruction of arable farm land continues at present levels. Today Canada is a net importer of food. Therefore two questions arise for consideration. First, we must ask how many people we can absorb in this country. Second, and more important, we must consider to what extent the "have" countries of the world, by exporting science and technology, have been able to help the "have-not" countries.
At present, Mr. Speaker, for every 100 Canadians we add to our population we destroy, on average, 1,000 acres of top grade arable farm land. At present Canada has three acres of agricultural land for every person in Canada. The world's average now is one acre of arable land for every person in the world. According to predictions, by the year 2000 Canada will have less than one acre of arable land for each of her citizens if present rates of farm land destruction should continue. Therefore if we have an open immigration policy Canada will be worse off by the year 2000 than the rest of the world is at present. We shall be worse off unless we redirect our immigrants to those areas where there is not high quality agricultural land.

Immigration Act
As an aside I might mention that many cities in this country have sprung up on our best land. For example on the prairies, the cities of Winnipeg, Regina, Saskatoon, Lethbridge, Red Deer, Edmonton and Grande Prairie-in fact all major cities except Medicine Hat and Calgary-are built on lake beds where the soil is silted over. That is a natural phenomenom since the pioneers found they could grow the best crops on that land. But it also means that we are using up the best land in Canada and rapidly destroying the base for our own food supplies. In the five years between 1966 and 1971, Canada lost 4.5 million acres of top quality farm land to urban growth. At the present rate of farm land destruction, 100 per cent of Ontario's farm land will be destroyed by AD 2030. Canada can best meet her humanitarian obligations not by importing people, but rather by exporting technology and research, and to that theme I wish to devote the remainder of my speech.
Let us consider how "have" countries in the world have made available research and technology to "have not" countries and enabled people of the Third World to become selfsufficient. I shall quote what Peter Jennings wrote in the September, 1976, edition of the Scientific American. He said:
In the 1940's Mexico had been importing half of the wheat it consumed in order to make up a deficit in production; yields averaged 750 kilograms per hectare. By 1956 the nation was self-sufficient in wheat in spite of a large increase in population. By 1970 yields had reached 3,200 kilograms per hectare.
That was a tremendous increase for that country.
I further quote from the same article by Peter Jennings:
By the mid-1960's the success of this program had been demonstrated, largely because of the broad environmental adaptation of the varieties. Beginning in 1966 seed was exported in quantity, mostly to India, Pakistan and Turkey. Record harvests were achieved almost immediately.
That is important to note. The fundamental question has to be who will help when the whole world becomes overcrowded? If we import people into technologically advanced nations today to such an extent that we all become Third World nations, the real question has to be who will be the saviour of mankind then?
I wish to quote further from the article in Scientific American which states, and I quote:
The first improved dwarf varieties of rice were released by 1RRI in 1966; they immediately transformed rice culture in the Philippines and were soon widely adopted in the lowland regions of Asia. One variety in particular, designated IR8, gained widespread celebrity. It has the potential for high yield when properly fertilized and cultivated, it is insensitive to photoperiod and it is adapted to a broad range of growing conditions. Moreover, it matures in 120 days instead of the 160 days required for many unimproved types. Because of the earlier maturity two crops a year can be grown in some regions.
I would further like to quote:
Genes that confer resistance to disease and insects have been bred into some of the better populations. As a result of these changes it has been possible to increase the crop density from 50,000 plants per hectare to more than 100,000.
I might just pause to point out that all of this data I am giving is to demonstrate that the gap in the narrowing of the food needs that exist in the Third World today is largely a gap that has come about because the "have" nations have been
able to export their science and technology to those poorer countries.
The point I intend to make today is simply this. As long as we have a policy that somehow will allow a flood of people to come into Canada, we have the two positions. First, we destroy our own position of strength. This in turn means there is no one to export that very much needed science and technology to the developing Third World. Canada has a lot more to contribute to assist in meeting the increasing world food need. I again quote:
Ralph W. Cummings of the Rockefeller Foundation recently published a survey of the state of food-crop technology in the low-income countries. He compared the average annual gain in production for 15 basic commodities during two periods, 1961 through 1965 and 1971 through 1973. His findings give a rough indication of the contribution of research to food production since World War II. Two conclusions emerge from the study. First an evaluation of the status of research on the major food crops indicates that in almost all cases research is "seriously inadequate" or "critically inadequate". Only the specialized areas of irrigated rice and irrigated spring wheat were considered to have received adequate research attention. Second, annual gains in production of seven crops (Cassava, white potato, soybeans, cowpeas, broad beans, maize and wheat) were greater than 2.5 per cent, and thus equaled or exceeded the rate of population growth.
In other words, if Canada is truly to become a humanitarian country, and without trying to think we are going to do something significant by an open immigration policy, we have to recognize our fundamental obligation, and that is to remain in a position of strength, and export science and technology to help the Third World people look after themselves.
The value of research and exported technology is easily demonstrated. This is a very important point. I again quote from the article in Scientific American:
The impact of the new technology is readily measured. Yield has risen from less than three metric tons per hectare to 5.4 metric tons, so that each hectare planted to the new varieties produces 2.5 metric tons of additional grain. Total production increased from 680,000 metric tons in 1966, the year before the program began, to 1,632,000 metric tons in 1975. Almost all the increase was accounted for by improved yield. The value of the additional crops harvested through 1974 was about $450 million. Varieties derived from the Colombian project were also successful in Mexico, Ecuador, Peru, Venezuela and in Central America. Throughout the region the 1974 harvest was increased by 1.5 million metric tons of grain.
What is being pointed out is that the gains we have made in the Third World, in levelling off the rate of starvation through increasing food production, have not happened because of increases in the amount of arable land but because of new research, science, and technology.
I go back to the fundamental question. If we are to have an open immigration policy and if the United States are to have a similar policy, somewhere down the road someone has to ask who is going to stop the starvation when all the countries of the world are in the same position?
There is no argument at all with the question of whether we ought to have a racist or non-racist policy. I hope it will be the assumption of all Canadians that we would not go along the lines of a racist policy. I see it will soon be four o'clock. I would simply say at this time that I think we can demonstrate categorically that Canada's strongest position in helping the Third World will be by the export of research and technology.

March 11, 1977

I hope to demonstrate that when I come back to this debate at the next opportunity. At this time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to call it four o'clock.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MEASURE TO RAISE HEALTH AND SAFETY STANDARDS FOR MINERS
speechtext:
Thai, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation which would establish a National Mining Act for the purpose of increasing occupational health standards for miners under federal jurisdiction, for establishing a federal presence in this particular area and to give leadership to provincial governments which do have responsibility for mine safety and occupational health.
He said: Mr. Speaker, one thing has struck me consistently since having been elected to this place. It is the consistency with which Canadians are being exposed to the propaganda of the mining corporations in Canada with regard to the major role of those companies in the Canadian economy. I am continuously being told that mining plays a major role in the Canadian economy.
In the year 1975 the total value of minerals extracted from the earth across Canada was $12 billion. This propaganda is delivered through all forms of the media; television, radio, newspapers, and magazines. It is delivered not only by individual mining companies but by their associations and clubs. These companies make one major argument, that if they are to stay healthy and competitive, the government must stay out of their business but give them more tax breaks, allowances, grants and so on. Well, Mr. Speaker, apart from the morality of this kind of advocacy advertising, the cost of which, incidentally, they can write off their taxes, there is the whole question of the workers who toil in the mining industry.
How safe is the mining industry in Canada? Who has responsibility for setting national mining safety standards across the country? Where does the responsibility of the
Mine Workers' Health
federal government begin and end, and where does the local responsibility begin and end? How strictly enforced are any standards of mining safety in areas for which the federal government has a direct responsibility? What is the cost of health care to the nation in respect of those who have become disabled or lost their lives in mining, and how much of this cost could have been prevented?
1 know the technique used by government members on the opposite side of the House in dealing with bills and motions put forward by private members. They get up, engage in much breast-beating, say they agree with the principles therein, and finally talk them out. I want to tell them that this motion does not threaten them in any way. All it says is that the House calls upon the government to consider a mining act of the kind proposed so that improved safety standards might come into effect. It is a motion which would have the effect of nudging the government to move in the direction I have outlined. The miners of this country demand no less from members on the government side than that they should allow the motion to come to a vote.
I ask members opposite, when they speak, to bear in mind that we have only an hour and that in all fairness to the workers they ought to let the matter come to a vote. I do not want to threaten them, but if they talk it out I will bring this debate to the attention of every union in this country, and to workers right across the country so that they will know who it is that bears the onus of standing against progress in this direction.

It is because of the questions I have just raised that I see a need for a national mining act. Apart from the fact that it would allow the central government and the provincial governments to sit down together and, with input from the trade union movement and the mining industry, devise an act which would clearly set out the federal and provincial areas of responsibility with respect to the mining industry, it would also provide a degree of protection for the Canadian miner which is urgently needed.
As I look across the country 1 see grave differences in working conditions in different areas. The miner in the Yukon has as much right to safety in his working place as does the miner in Ontario. At the present time workers are denied uniform levels of safety because of differing standards imposed by the provinces and even by federal departments. The federal government has responsibility for mines on Indian reservations, on military bases, and in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. Regulation of these different mines is handled in part by Energy, Mines and Resources, in part by Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and in part by the Atomic Energy Control Board.

In the north, in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, safety in mines is governed by mining safety ordinances. These can be set down by the Commissioner of the Territories but must be approved in Ottawa by the governor in council. These ordinances fall under the authority of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. In the Yukon and the Northwest Territories the federal government exercises control over mining comparable to the powers exercised by provinces within their own boundaries.
The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources also exercises broad powers, controlling such acts as the Explosives Act, the Atomic Energy Control Act, the Dominion Coal Board Act, and several other measures related to mining.
Mines in provinces are generally controlled by provincial governments, and within the various jurisdictions there are many different acts and regulations. Some provinces have enacted very advanced mining regulations and occupational health regulations, while others lag far behind.
A subject of great concern lately, and justifiably so, is the mining of uranium. Here the Atomic Energy Control Board has authority. The Board controls the production, manufacture, sale and use of radioactive material. But while theoretically controlling all this, the Board in fact does not. Instead, it has chosen to turn the exercise of these powers over to the provinces, thus washing its hands of the problem.
Recently in Ontario a commission was established to inquire into the health and safety of workers in mines-the Hamm Commission. AECB officials told that royal commission they had never asked the Ontario government for reports on levels of radiation in the mines or for the status of health of the miners. Commissioner James Hamm went so far as to charge that the Board was ignoring the miners, whose daily exposure to harmful radiation was, "larger than that received by workers around reactors." The AECB has not even declared uranium miners to be "workers" for the purpose of regulation by the federal government. The Commissioner raised many other questions in this area but I shall content myself with quoting one statement of his: "At times it has not been clear whether initiative was considered to rest with the industry or with the responsible ministry." To that, he might have added "and to precisely which responsible ministry."
The guidelines concerning safety differ in the different provinces and they also differ from the federal rules. For example, federal regulations state there shall be no more than 10 picocuries per litre of drinking water. In Ontario, provincial regulations state that the acceptable level is three. Let us not forget that in the Elliot Lake area leachings from radioactive mine tailings are threatening Indian bands and the town of Elliot Lake itself.
These safety regulations involve more than just plain numbers. Human lives are at stake. The AECB follows the guidelines set by the International Commission on Radiological Protection. This is the group which said 10 picocuries per litre of drinking water was an acceptable figure. People within the Board say the only reason the provincial figure is lower is because the province has not gotten around to raising them to

"more realistic levels". I wonder about that, Mr. Speaker. I wonder about it very much as reports continue to come in about lung cancer and silicosis among uranium miners.
Ontario is not the only province which has experienced problems in this regard. Saskatchewan was concerned about safety levels in uranium mines in that province. On January 29, 1975, the department concerned wrote to the Atomic Energy Control Board and asked that three inspectors be appointed by that board to launch a system of safety inspection. Saskatchewan acted in this way out of disgust with the federal government's failure to set standards and inspect mines at Uranium City. The letter had not even been answered by November of 1976. When steel workers asked the Board why the letter had not been answered they were told it was because the Board had not had the time. I wonder how many more people will die before we can find the time to do something about health and safety in these mines.
The leader of my party, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whit-by (Mr. Broadbent), has moved three private members' bills in this House which would do much to cut down on the problem of occupational health for workers under federal jurisdiction. His bills would provide health and safety committees in all work places with ten or more employees; they would provide for mandatory work inspectors, and would allow workers the right to refuse work they considered dangerous. Those bills would help a great deal in cutting down the carnage in our work places. They might even reduce the number of injured workers in the post office. But in the case of mining I think we must go even further.
Mining is a dangerous and thankless occupation. I recall that we argued for months in this House over the merits of capital punishment and concern as to whether or not guards or policemen would be killed. We heard about the great risks that guards and policemen face as they try to carry out their duties. We should remember that, when it comes to hazardous occupations, a miner still has a greater chance of being killed than either a prison guard or a policeman.
Perhaps it is time, Mr. Speaker, we took some steps to do something about the problem. A national mining act would bring the issue before the public. We could examine in depth the measures needed to protect our miners from Newfoundland to British Columbia. Not only would such an act simplify the acts and regulations of different departments, but it would also provide for more adequate standards and inspections. It would also put pressure on the provinces to accept more adequate measures in areas where their legislation falls below federal standards.
We owe it to our miners, and their families to legislate the highest possible standards for their health and protection. Anything less is a travesty in view of and genuine concern for the Canadian working class.

The other member of that party present this afternoon indicates they are unanimous. As 1 interpret the motion of the hon. member, he wishes the government, if I may read part of it, to consider the advisability of introducing legislation for the purpose of increasing occupational health standards for miners under federal jurisdiction, for establishing a federal presence in this particular area, and to give leadership to provincial governments which do have responsibility for mine safety and occupational health.
I purposely omitted in reading those words the actual term "National Mining Act", and I did so for a very good reason. It seems to me that in order to achieve the very creditable aim the hon. member for Nickel Belt has in mind, which is to focus increasing government attention at the federal level on the problems of safety related to people in industry generally, he has focused solely upon one area. My own feeling is that this whole area of occupational health and safety is something that needs to be addressed on a much grander scale than simply dealing with one particular industry. So while I agree with the substance of the hon. member's objective, and indeed have no problem supporting him-1 hope he will continue to push his point of view-in my opinion the idea of trying to establish a mining act as such to deal with only one very narrow area of the problem is not the most appropriate way to proceed.
Again in my view, Mr. Speaker, it is great to see something like this being discussed without seeing a headline in the paper the previous day. In other words, my concern is that governments have tended to react in this area of occupational health and safety only after major tragedies, or more recently where we have seen more insidious types of tragedies where one or two miners are known to be afflicted by diseases which seem to have emanated from their terms of service in the mines. For this reason 1 feel privileged to participate in a debate which is going to tackle this problem in a sensible and, I hope, coordinated way.
I should like to review a little bit of background to show what has happened in this whole area of occupational health hazards on this continent. It seems to me that, whether we like it or not, we are very often inclined to look to others who perhaps have been in business longer than we have in terms of some of our national industries and have had more resources at hand, and consequently started to deal with some of these problems earlier than we have. I refer to the United States.
Mine Workers' Health
As I understand it, the oldest act in the United States is the Walsh-Healey Act, which was established to create standards of occupational health in those areas where companies were dealing in contracts with the federal government. As I understand it, various types of individual standards existed throughout the various states, and in some states standards were non-existent. I do not know when this act was passed, but it was a good while ago and it was a very important first step.
I put this information on the record, Mr. Speaker, because it seems to me that we in Canada have a long way to go. We are starting from ground zero almost, as it were, so I think it is important that we do review what has happened in this major country to the south of us.
Two additional acts have been passed in the United States, and one of these was the coal mining safety and health act which reacted to public concern over what is known as "black lung" in the Pennsylvania and Kentucky coal mining areas. This particular piece of legislation was designed to provide equitable compensation for people who were afflicted with this condition as a result of their work environment. I understand that through this act a very important body was created known as the national institute for occupational safety and health in the health, education and welfare department of that country. Again I am not sure of the timing of the introduction of this particular act, but it was another very important cornerstone in the over-all effort made in the country to the south of us to attempt to come to grips with occupational health standards and their establishment.
Then we have an act known as the mining environment safety administration act, which was administered by mines people and was passed, I believe, in 1972. Whereas they had focused primarily on the area the hon. member for Nickel Belt is dealing with, one specific narrow area, they were now obliged to go outside the coal mining area and to move into more general mining fields, which I gather included hardrock and mines other than coal generally. Standards were established under this act for silica and explosive gases.
1 myself had some very brief but interesting inter-action as a member of a parliamentary committee which went to Washington a year and a half ago in another area related to occupational safety and health, and this was through my discussions with senior officials in the occupational safety and health administration under their department of labour. Again I put this information on the record because it seems to me we are seeing a rather large mix of various areas of responsibility trying to get at the same problem. I am relating how the situation has developed in the United States, and I am not sure that they are entirely happy with it. Nevertheless, this particular focus under the U.S. Department of Labour, which is the most recent of all that have been established, covers up to 60 million workers in that country in five million work places. They employ a staff of 2,000, which gives you some indication of the type of bureaucracy involved. In talking with the senior people involved in this administration we found that in their view this was perhaps the biggest single piece of social legislation that had been introduced in the United States in recent

speechtext:
The occupational and safety health act. Initially it was aimed at safety, but now-when I say "now" I am saying so on the basis of my notes made in the autumn of 1975-they are moving to develop international standards in the area of health in work places in general. They are very actively co-operating with the state authorities. This was the question we put to them, knowing that in this country the jurisdiction is mainly provincial. To some degree the same applies in the United States, and they are having to work closely with individual state authorities. This is an agency within the department of labour.
Moving closer to home and to the heart of the problem pointed out by the hon. member for Nickel Belt, let me draw attention to the throne speech of October 12 in which the following was indicated. This is an extract which reads:
An industrial safety and health centre will be established to assist companies and workers in their efforts to identify any remove hazards.
The government will work closely with its own employees in various departments and Crown corporations to implement innovative, co-operative methods of improving health and safety conditions.
I have attempted to bring myself up to date on what may have developed in that area since that indication of prospective legislation was given to us in the throne speech, and I understand from talking to people in the industrial area that something called the Canada Centre for Occupational Safety and Health is being seriously considered, and already government people are circulating around the country talking to people from industry, labour and provincial governments in an effort to come up with some basic co-ordination in the area of health. The idea is to combine not just the problems related to mining but all the problems relating to safety and health standards, such as problems found in the agricultural sector, the mining sector, atomic energy, and the industrial sector generally. The idea is to establish national leadership in this area, and there is a good deal of sympathy among the provinces for this type of leadership to take place.
I understand that there are four basic problems that should be studied initially. One is the problem of silicosis, or exposure to dust, which is primarily a mining problem but which can be encountered in many other industries as well. The second one is a matter of noise, and the problem associated particularly in the mining field with underground drilling and other types of mining operations. There is also the problem of lung cancer from radioactive elements. We have heard much more about this as some of the problems have surfaced and are being discussed and studied in great depth. Fourth, there is the matter of underground diesels and the fumes created by them. I gather that these are the four areas which are being considered initially by this team travelling across the country, and I have this from people with whom that team has interacted rather than from government sources. There is a general

feeling among these people that something is finally going to be done and that some leadership will be shown at the federal level.
There is a tradition in this country similar to what the Americans faced when they tried to move in this area, that safety and health are a responsibility of the provinces. The indication to date is that everyone is anxious to respond to federal leadership in this area.
I have a little more to say on this centre, Mr. Speaker, the idea is to establish a place where a scientific background can be developed for establishing valid standards for the use of hazardous substances and chemicals such as, for instance, asbestos. Nobody really knew anything about the threshold limits in this area. It is an open area. We hope the centre will come to grips with this problem and will establish threshold figures acceptable to all parties concerned. Incidentally the agency will be directed by representatives from labour, management, and the provincial and federal governments. It is to be a kind of clearing house. Universities may be involved in the studies. It will not necessarily employ a large bureaucracy, but might farm out studies to various centres in the country where they could more appropriately be undertaken. It will act as a focal point for encouraging research and for setting standards.
As I understand it, ultimately there will be legislation in this area once the team has been able to pool together its various reports from the current studies it is undertaking and the consultations it is having across the country. It is my hope that this legislation will incorporate the very points the hon. member for Nickel Belt mentioned today. This is why I say that I think in the long run hon. members will be better served by a more encompassing piece of legislation which will cover all aspects of industrial hazards, rather than spending a great deal of time on one narrow area. I hope the hon. member for Nickel Belt will continue his interest in that area and will take an interest in larger and more encompassing legislation when it comes forward.
In conclusion I would like to make some reference to the Hamm report of which many of us are aware. It is a provincial study which was undertaken through the auspices of the Ontario government. It is a critical report. It criticizes both labour and industry for failing to live up to their responsibilities and insure safety in mines at that time. I think federal legislation will surely draw on that report and incorporate the points from that report which should be included in a more encompassing piece of legislation.
I am also conscious of the fact mentioned by the hon. member for Nickel Belt that, as he put it, those of us who rose to speak on this issue should be chastized. I want to point out to him that basically I am in support of the substance of his bill, but I do not support the means by which he is attempting to achieve his objective.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great care to the beginning of the speech of the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin), and I heard those magic words we hear in private members' hour from hon. members on the government side to the effect that they basically support certain matters. If that is the case, especially when we are dealing with a motion and not a bill, and if hon. members opposite generally support this resolution, which deals specifically with the occupational health standards and problems of miners working under the jurisdiction of the federal government, a government which is supported and propped up by hon. members opposite, one of whom just spoke, they will allow this motion to pass. If that is the case, I am pleased. 1 am prepared to support this motion, and I commend the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) for bringing it forward.
Some may ask why a member from the national capital area should support a motion regarding mining. It goes without saying that there are very few mines in the national capital area. I dare say there are very few mines in the borough of Scarborough either.
I have some credentials-albeit somewhat distant-with respect to the operation of mines in Canada. Technology has changed, but my experience is still vivid in my memory. When I was a student at law school I worked for a portion of a year underground in a gold mine in the Schumacher area of Ontario. I worked in Stopes. I was a raise man. I ran a mucking machine. I even drove a train until I wrecked it one day, and I was not allowed to operate the train underground after that. I am glad I caused some of my colleagues to smile this afternoon, but that is the truth. I saw at first hand the working of a mine.
Working in a mine is by its nature dangerous. It differs from other occupations in which there is some aspect of danger, but working in a mine is dangerous in itself. A person can be physically injured if he is tired or if he allows himself to be unaware of what is happening around him for just a moment. The atmosphere in which mine workers carry out their duties is dangerous. There are fumes, dust and other things in mines which are injurious.
If the hon. member for Scarborough West was speaking for the majority in this Elouse when he said he basically supports
Mine Workers' Health
this measure-and I am sure he must have been-I hope the matter will proceed so that study of this matter can take place in the appropriate committee. I hope today through this motion the House will express support for taking steps to raise occupational health standards for miners.
We tend to think of mining as being under provincial jurisdiction, and it is. There are some very sophisticated standards in the various provinces of Canada. They vary from one province to another, but in Ontario there is some considerable sophistication which has been viewed critically in the Hamm report. Perhaps that is a good thing. Out of that there may be some action taken in terms of mining in Ontario.
However, there is a considerable amount of mining taking place in the Yukon Territory and in the Northwest Territories. That industry is likely to grow as we look more and more to those areas for resources to be used for national purposes. I do not believe it will be possible for any responsible federal government which has jurisdiction over those territories to leave the question of mine safety to ordinances of the territorial councils, as well intentioned as they may be.
I gather that is the thrust of the hon. member's motion. There will be a day when those territories will be provinces, and then we hope they will have the resources to develop criteria with respect to mining and a host of other things, but they do not have those resources now. Therefore they depend on the federal government-their mother and father, so to speak-for that kind of guidance. That being so, there is a case to be made for a national mining act.
With respect to the argument that this kind of thing was dealt with in the throne speech, of course it was dealt with in the throne speech, but these things are a long time coming, for one reason or another. There may be a good administrative reason for this, although it is unknown to me. I do not want this to be a partisan day, but I think we have a responsibility in this House today in a non-partisan way to urge the government, by agreeing to this motion, to speed things up. We are not dealing with statistics, we are dealing with men and women who are involved directly or indirectly in the mining industry, and I hope hon. members on the government side will recognize the important human problem which is involved.
The last argument made by the hon. member opposite, who said at the same time he basically supports this motion, was that the focus of the motion is too narrow. The motion focuses on an immediate problem. In the federal territories there is no particular industrial safety problem compared with the magnitude of the problems there are in the mining industry. If the hon. member needs a reason for the narrow focus of the motion, that is a good reason, and if he wants to look to precedent, he can look to the precedents in all the provinces of Canada where mining is dealt with separately and other industries are dealt with separately because there are unique problems in each. However, that is not a reason to wait, and I hope hon. members opposite will consider this matter.
It really is a tragedy that we tend to wait for some major upheaval before we look at the mining industry or any other industry in which tragedies occur. There is no immediate

March 11, 1977
Mine Workers' Health
problem at the moment in the federal territories, but this is a good opportunity for this House to express its concern about possible problems.
We tend to think of mining only in the traditional sense of mining from the surface of the earth upon which man can walk, and machines move down into the ground to extract minerals. According to information given to us yesterday at an interparliamentary union luncheon, we are now in the process of considering technology for mining the seabed in more or less the traditional sense of the word. We are speaking in terms of removing nodules from the seabed. That is a whole new technology, and I think there is an opportunity for us to keep safety legislation parallel with and up to the technology we are developing.
I commend the hon. member for Nickel Belt. I do not often do that, but he has touched a problem with which I have some experience. I commend him for bringing this motion forward and I hope the House will support it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any question that we are going to talk this motion out because we do have something to say about it. We support the notion but not necessarily the motion. We think there are better ways of dealing with the same problem. It would be almost impossible to get a national mining act through this House because of the constitutional aspect of the question. We believe there are other approaches, and we have taken steps which make rather more sense than this motion, certainly until constitutional changes are brought about.
I have some concern that the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) has virtually threatened members if we talk this motion out. I consider that a kind of blackmail and it disturbs me a great deal. It is an unparliamentary approach to this matter.
The hon. member has more experience in a mining community than I, although I have worked and lived near mining communities. I understand his concern because there is no more depressed community in this country than a depressed mining community. The hon. member lives near one of the wealthiest, but many of the smaller ones are one industry towns and local tax revenues are poor, as are amenities for the miners. There is a good deal of movement back and forth as people take jobs for only a short period of time. It is an industry which is not itself depressed, but an industry where the people are depressed. I accept this and I am concerned about it. One of the reasons for this is that mining and natural resources are provincial concerns, and it may be easier for a large corporation to manipulate the provinces than the federal government. This is something that members of his party have said on many occasions.
The motion deals with health and safety in the main, but it also deals with a federal presence in the area of mining. I am concerned about some of the things that have happened or are

happening in northern Ontario, such as the closing of the asbestos mine in Matachewan in the past ten days. A good deal of work was done regarding this particular mine by the hon. member's party. I understand that the Ontario leader of the party now says that mine is in good shape but it has been closed because it has no money. According to an article in the Ottawa Citizen on March 9, the chairman of the company said:
We had $35 million in hand from U.S. financial institutions to refund our outstanding loans until the lead company-an insurance firm-met the premier the morning before the speech.
He added:
They pulled out of the arrangement with us right afterwards.
This seems to be one of the problems, although part of the difficulty is that this mine is related to ownership of a mine in Quebec. As a result of the closing, 300 jobs were lost. This is a golden opportunity for the federal government to become involved, because through the Canada Development Corporation and ownership of the Texas Gulf Company we have properties near by. It would seem to be a natural area where the CDC could move in because of these valuable assets. In addition to the 300 people out of work, suppliers and subsuppliers etc. are also suffering.
This is a national problem and it needs a national solution, yet there are constitutional barriers which prevent action. I can suggest one way, through the CDC, in which the federal government can become involved.
In northwestern Ontario there are a number of small mines and many of us think they should be worked if there are valuable resources in them, especially when prices are better than they were when they closed. However, there is a need for things like portable mills and money for the small operator in order that these mines can be reworked. There are capable people available, and yet there does not seem to be support, national or otherwise, for any but major operations.
Transportation is another problem. At one INCO mine, a major line of the CNR passes within a mile or so and yet the ore is being hauled out by truck on a road that was especially built.
I would suggest that the federal government should play a larger role in the mining industry, but I know we have a very difficult problem. Both opposition parties have said that the provinces must be supreme and that we must not take these industries away from the provinces. With the oil industry, which is akin to mining, we are reminded that it is a provincial resource and that the federal government has no business interfering. On the other hand, both oppostion parties now tell us that the federal government ought to get into the mining area.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MEASURE TO RAISE HEALTH AND SAFETY STANDARDS FOR MINERS
speechtext:
Matters related to the occupational safety and health of miners and workers engaged in associated surface operations are subject to existing legislation and regulations, federal, provincial, and territorial. The content and administration of these statutory requirements are reviewed from time to time by the regulatory authorities concerned, and are revised as required. Federal jurisdiction for these purposes in the mining industry is, by acts of parliament, confined to the mining and processing of uranium, coal mining carried out by the Cape Breton Development Corporation, and the mining of base metals in the Flin Flon mineral area by the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company.
Part IV of the Canada Labour Code, safety of employees, and the safety and health regulations made pursuant to it, apply to all aspects of occupational safety and health in federal works, undertakings and businesses except where such application is preempted, as for example by the Atomic Energy Control Act. Workers under federal jurisdiction in occupations directly involved in the mining of coal, uranium, and base metals are under the general regulations of Part IV of the Canada Labour Code, regulations made under the Atomic Energy Control Act and, by arrangement, the mining regulations of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario.
To take a portion of workers and work places under federal jurisdiction, for example, miners and mines, and make them subject to a new act of parliament and regulations resulting therefrom would in effect duplicate the existing provisions of
Mine Workers' Health
Part IV of the Canada Labour Code and of the Atomic Energy Control Act and might result in delaying the development and implementation of higher standards through revision of existing enactments and mandatory standards.
A federal presence in the field of occupational safety and health of miners already exists through the implementation of the regulations made under Part IV of the Canada Labour Code in coal mines and regulations made under the Atomic Energy Control Act in uranium mining operations.
Assistance to and co-operation with provincial departments and agencies that have a responsibility for mine safety and occupational health is considered to be an important and ongoing function of the federal government, and there are established means for consultation and sharing of information among the several interests and authorities. As the hon. member for Scarborough West indicated, active consideration is being given to the creation of a National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health which, as its name implies, would be a technically competent and authoritative body for the identification and evaluation of hazards to the safety and health of workers, and to develop standards and other means for their control. Such a centre would be governed by a board representing federal and provincial authorities, labour, management, scientific and other professional interests. Through the work and efforts of an institute of this kind it is confidently expected that higher standards of occupational safety and health would be developed and implemented for all places of work-I emphasize all places of work-including mining which has its own special problems in this field.
